design_detail: Steady-state pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic study over one 24-hour dosing interval in 18 people on stable once-daily methadone in the South Australian public methadone maintenance programme: 9 who reported no withdrawal between doses ('holders') and 9 who reported regular withdrawal before the next dose ('nonholders'), admitted to the programme's inpatient unit. Plasma racemic methadone was measured 13 times and withdrawal and opioid effects 11 times; 10 drug-free controls had the same effect measures without methadone or blood samples. Holders and nonholders compared with t tests; sigmoid Emax concentration-effect models. Read as the published PDF, Clin Pharmacol Ther 1999;65:685-694.
can_establish: Whether, in these 18 people on stable methadone, withdrawal symptoms rose and fell with plasma methadone over one dosing interval, and whether those who reported withdrawal before the next dose differed from those who did not in their level just before the dose, their overall exposure (AUC) or how fast their levels fell after the peak.
cannot_establish: That a faster fall in methadone levels causes withdrawal between doses (one interval, 9 per group, groups formed by self-report, the key difference significant only after excluding 2 people); how common such withdrawal is (the one-third figure comes from the authors' earlier survey, not this sample); or whether any change in treatment helps (none was tested).

sample.recruitment: Volunteers enrolled in the South Australian Public Methadone Maintenance Program for at least 6 months (range 6 months to 10 years) with no dose change for at least 2 months; 10 volunteer controls (p. 686).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Excluded: pregnancy and positive HIV serology. How holder or nonholder status was established is not described beyond self-report (p. 686).
sample.demographics: 11 men and 7 women, aged 21-45 years, 60-94 kg. Holders and nonholders: age 36.3 and 34.3 years, time in the programme 2.3 and 3.9 years, weight 71.7 and 76.7 kg, men 67% and 56%, none significantly different (p. 690). Controls' ages and weights within the patients' range (p. 686).
sample.attrition: None reported. Concentration-effect models could be fitted for withdrawal in 9 of 18 people, for the MBG score in 10, pupil diameter in 12, pain threshold in 4 and respiratory rate in none (p. 690).
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected volunteers grouped by their own report, from one programme, long in treatment and stable; people with HIV excluded. The earlier survey the authors cite (34% of 114 patients were nonholders, p. 686) is not this sample.

exposure.measurement: Supervised dosing in the unit; plasma racemic methadone by HPLC (quantification limit 30 ng/mL; inter- and intra-assay inaccuracy under 8%) before the dose and 12 times over 23 hours; AUC by the linear trapezoidal method, peak and trough by inspection, and the maximum hourly rate of decline from peak to trough for each person (pp. 686-687).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: oral methadone syrup once daily at each person's usual stable dose, 0.12-1.9 mg/kg (7.5-130 mg) (p. 686); doses by group are not reported. In treatment at least 6 months, dose unchanged at least 2 months.
exposure.polysubstance: Most smoked cigarettes; urine positive for cannabinoids in 10, opioids other than methadone in 2, amphetamines in 2 and barbiturates in 1; 4 drank alcohol regularly, under 40 g a day; drug-positive urine did not differ between holders and nonholders (p. 686). The 2 with other opioids were holders and were excluded post hoc from one comparison (p. 690). Controls had used no psychoactive drug other than nicotine or caffeine for 2 months.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: people were tested on their usual methadone; other drug use was checked only by urinalysis.

comparison.controls: Main comparison: holders against nonholders. The 10 drug-free controls served only as a reference for the effect measures; they received no methadone and gave no blood (p. 686).
comparison.matching: Controls within the patients' ranges of age and weight; holders and nonholders not matched.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Methadone dose by group, years of opioid use before treatment, metabolic or genetic differences, other medicines, mood and anxiety, and expectations (people knew their own label).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Drug-free apart from nicotine and caffeine.

outcomes.instruments: Methadone Symptoms Checklist (the authors' 1997 instrument), withdrawal score 0-16; Morphine-Benzedrine Group scale of the Addiction Research Center Inventory (16 yes/no items) for positive opioid effects; pupil diameter from video under constant light; respiratory and pulse rate by observation; pain threshold to an electrical stimulus to the ear lobe (p. 687).
outcomes.validity_norms: The MBG scale is described as valid and reliable; no validity data are given for the withdrawal checklist.
outcomes.operationalization: Withdrawal severity is the number of withdrawal symptoms reported. A nonholder is a person who reports regular withdrawal during the dosing interval. The pharmacokinetic predictor is the maximum hourly fall in plasma methadone from peak to trough.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Five effect measures at up to 11 times by two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, at least five pharmacokinetic comparisons by t test, correlations and four sets of model parameters.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; the subjective measures were self-reported by people who knew which group they were in.

analysis.effect_sizes: Holders against nonholders (means, labelled as SD): plasma methadone before the dose 249 against 257 ng/mL (P > .05; range 44-614); peak-to-trough ratio 1.9 ± 0.1 against 1.7 ± 0.1 (P > .05); AUC 7.4 ± 5.0 against 8.2 ± 3.9 mg·h/L (P > .05). Maximum rate of decline 47.6 ± 21.3 against 74.5 ± 40.4 ng/mL/h, t = 1.77, P = .09; without 2 holders with other opioids in urine, 42.1 ± 20.8 against 74.5 ± 40.4, t = 2.10, stated P < .05 (two-sided P about .054 on 14 degrees of freedom, editors' calculation). Maximum rate of decline against withdrawal symptoms from peak to trough: r = 0.60 in all 18 (P < .01 in the text, P < .001 in the legend; about .009 by editors' calculation), r = 0.67 without the 2 (stated P < .001; about .005). Slope factors N: withdrawal 5.4 ± 0.9, MBG 5.1 ± 1.05, pupil 1.2 ± 0.1, pain threshold 2.8 ± 0.7, with no holder-nonholder differences (Table I).
analysis.preregistration_detail: None reported; ethics approval from the Royal Adelaide Hospital Research Ethics Committee (p. 686).
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract reports the subset comparison (74.5 against 42.1 ng/mL/h) as the group difference, without saying that two people were left out or that the full comparison was not significant (P = .09) (p. 685).
analysis.power: Not reported; 9 per group, and the concentration-effect comparisons rest on 4 to 7 people per group (Table I).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 18 people on stable methadone, withdrawal symptoms went down as plasma methadone rose and came back as it fell, with very steep concentration-effect curves for withdrawal and positive effects. Those reporting withdrawal before the next dose had the same level just before the dose and the same AUC as those who did not; their levels fell faster after the peak, a difference significant only after a post hoc exclusion of two people, with a two-sided P just above .05 by the editors' calculation.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that clinically important withdrawal is 'a consequence of more rapid decline in methadone concentration' (p. 685), and the Discussion that the differences 'are a consequence of pharmacokinetic rather than pharmacodynamic differences' (p. 692): causal conclusions from one dosing interval in 18 people, with the pharmacodynamic comparison resting on 4 to 7 people per group and the key difference on a subset. The Discussion also extends the 34% from the authors' earlier survey to other clinics and draws recommendations about dose scheduling and alternative medicines that this study did not test, while warning that data on the racemic mixture call for great caution about the mechanism (p. 692).

timeline.event: Nilsson et al.: smaller distribution volume and shorter half-life in people on methadone maintenance judged therapeutic failures (as described on p. 686; not read).
Hiltunen et al.: plasma methadone correlated with subjective withdrawal, less with objective measures (as described on p. 691; not read).

Dyer and White, the same group: 34% of 114 patients in the same programme reported regular withdrawal between doses, with no difference in demographics, other drug use or time in treatment (as described on p. 686; not read).
This study: first concurrent measurement of plasma methadone and withdrawal across a dosing interval in holders and nonholders.

replication.where_it_stands: Earlier studies cited by the authors point the same way (withdrawal follows falling methadone levels; people with poor responses clear or redistribute methadone differently), but no later replication of the holder-nonholder difference in the rate of decline was read for this card, and the enantiomer analysis the authors announced was not read.

funding.funder: Royal Adelaide Hospital Research Committee; scholarships to two authors (a Dawes Scholarship from the Royal Adelaide Hospital and a Dora Lush Postgraduate Scholarship from the NHMRC; a National Drug Strategy Postgraduate Research Scholarship) (p. 685).
funding.affiliations_note: University of Adelaide (clinical and experimental pharmacology; psychology) and the Royal Adelaide Hospital.

what_would_settle_it: A larger study of people on methadone, with withdrawal between doses measured on a standard scale rather than by self-label, the analysis planned in advance, R-methadone (the active enantiomer) measured, and doses reported by group; then randomized comparisons of treatment options for people who report such withdrawal.

domains.note: No adjustment; methadone dose by group not reported; other drug use present (two with other opioids); groups similar only on age, weight, sex and time in treatment.
Plasma methadone by a validated HPLC assay at 13 times during supervised steady-state dosing.
Volunteers chosen by self-reported holder status; two holders excluded post hoc from the key comparison.
Usual dose, supervised, during one inpatient day.
Concentration-effect models fitted in only 9 of 18 for withdrawal and 4 for pain; people without a fit were dropped from those analyses.
Withdrawal self-reported on the authors' checklist by people who knew their label; no blinding reported.
The key difference is significant only in a post hoc subset that the abstract presents as the result; several P values do not match their test statistics.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A small, carefully measured pharmacokinetic study whose main group comparison is fragile: the two groups were formed by self-report, the rate-of-decline difference was not significant in the full sample (P = .09) and borderline after excluding two people, and the abstract reports only the subset. The within-person link between falling levels and withdrawal (r = 0.60 across all 18) is the sturdier finding. The study can be cited for that link and for the absence of a difference in levels just before the dose; it cannot be cited as showing that a faster fall causes withdrawal, or for any treatment change.

key_findings.finding: Sample: 9 self-reported holders and 9 nonholders on once-daily methadone, in treatment 6 months to 10 years, dose unchanged at least 2 months; 11 men and 7 women, aged 21-45; most smoked; urine positive for cannabinoids in 10, other opioids in 2, amphetamines in 2, barbiturates in 1; 10 drug-free controls.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Patients and control subjects, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Over the dosing interval, withdrawal symptoms were significantly more frequent in the 18 patients than in controls at all times and least severe from 2 to about 8 hours after the dose; the MBG positive-effect score peaked 2-3 hours after the dose and returned to baseline by 7 hours; pain threshold was raised for about 6 hours; pupils were smaller than in controls throughout; respiratory rate fell 3 hours after the dose and was faster than in controls before the dose and from about 9 hours after it.
key_findings.locator: Results › Pharmacodynamic responses: Subjective responses and Objective responses paragraphs; Figure 1 legend (p. 688)

key_findings.finding: Withdrawal was significantly higher in nonholders and strongly inversely related to plasma methadone in both groups. Plasma methadone before the dose: 249 ng/mL in holders and 257 ng/mL in nonholders (P > .05; range 44-614); 6 of 9 in each group were above 200 ng/mL. Peaks at about 3 hours, not different, range 69-980 ng/mL. Peak-to-trough ratio 1.9 ± 0.1 and 1.7 ± 0.1 (P > .05). AUC 7.4 ± 5.0 and 8.2 ± 3.9 mg·h/L (P > .05). AUC correlated with weight-adjusted dose (r = 0.74, P < .001).
key_findings.locator: Results › Pharmacokinetics and withdrawal severity in holders and nonholders, 1st paragraph; Figure 2

key_findings.finding: Maximum rate of decline in plasma methadone: holders 47.6 ± 21.3 and nonholders 74.5 ± 40.4 ng/mL/h (t = 1.77, P = .09); without the two people with other opioids in urine, 42.1 ± 20.8 against 74.5 ± 40.4 (t = 2.10, stated P < .05). Correlation between maximum rate of decline and mean number of withdrawal symptoms from peak to trough in all 18: r = 0.60 (P < .01); without the two, r = 0.67 (P < .001).
key_findings.locator: Results › Pharmacokinetics and withdrawal severity, 2nd paragraph; Figure 3 and legend
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: t = 2.10 on 14 degrees of freedom gives two-sided P of about .054; r = 0.67 with 16 people gives P of about .005. The two excluded people were holders (the nonholder values are unchanged).

key_findings.finding: Slope factors N (Table I): withdrawal 5.4 ± 0.9 (holders 6.1, n = 4; nonholders 4.9, n = 5), MBG 5.1 ± 1.05 (n = 10), pupil diameter 1.2 ± 0.1 (n = 12), pain threshold 2.8 ± 0.7 (n = 4); EC50 for withdrawal 301.8 ± 292.1 ng/mL; no holder-nonholder differences (P > .05). N differed between withdrawal and pupil diameter (P < .0001), MBG and pupil (P < .006), pain and pupil (P < .007), but not withdrawal and pain (P < .054).
key_findings.locator: Results › Plasma concentration-effect relationships, 1st paragraph (p. 690); Table I (p. 691)

key_findings.finding: Background from the authors' earlier survey in the same programme: 34% of a non-selected sample of 114 patients regularly experienced withdrawal between doses, with average daily doses above 60 mg and no differences in demographics, other drug use or time in the programme; plasma levels were not measured there.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand within this paper (Dyer and White, 1997, not read).

key_findings.finding: The authors draw recommendations about dose scheduling and alternative medicines (buprenorphine, LAAM, slow-release morphine, a slow-release methadone) and caution that analyses of racemic methadone call for great caution about the mechanism; none of the recommendations was tested in this study.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph (caution) and 7th paragraph (recommendations)
key_findings.note: The scheduling recommendation is not reproduced here (no regimens on the site).

reporting_issues.issue: The subset comparison of the maximum rate of decline (42.1 ± 20.8 for 7 holders against 74.5 ± 40.4 for 9 nonholders, t = 2.10) is reported as P < .05; on 14 degrees of freedom the two-sided P is about .054 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The only reported pharmacokinetic difference between the groups is borderline even after a post hoc exclusion; it is not significant in the full sample (P = .09).

reporting_issues.issue: For r = 0.60 in 18 patients the text gives P < .01 and the Figure 3 legend P < .001 (about .009 by editors' calculation); for r = 0.67 in 16 the text gives P < .001 (about .005).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the correlations hold at P < .01.

reporting_issues.issue: Values are labelled mean ± SD (p. 689; Table I), but the peak-to-trough ratios 1.9 ± 0.1 and 1.7 ± 0.1 with P > .05 fit standard errors (with SDs of 0.1 and 9 per group, P would be below .001), and the all-patient slope factors for MBG and pupil diameter equal the standard errors of the pooled subgroup values (editors' calculation); the withdrawal row (5.4 ± 0.9) fits neither.
reporting_issues.consequence: Variability between people is larger than the table suggests; the ± values cannot be read as SDs without checking.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives the maximal rate of decline as 74.5 against 42.1 ng/mL/h (p. 685), the subset values, without saying that two people were excluded or that the full-sample comparison (47.6 against 74.5) was not significant.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader of the abstract alone would overrate the group difference.

reporting_issues.issue: Methadone doses are given only as a range for all 18 (7.5-130 mg; p. 686), not by group.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether holders and nonholders differed in dose cannot be checked; similar AUCs (p. 690) only partly address this.

design_detail: Systematic review and bivariate random-effects meta-analysis of 19 cohort studies (20 articles published 1974–2016, all from high-income countries: 11 Europe/Israel, 4 North America, 4 Australia) of people with opioid dependence who received methadone maintenance (18 cohorts, 122,885 participants, follow-up 1965–2010) or buprenorphine maintenance (3 cohorts, 15,831 participants, 1990–2010). Crude all-cause and overdose death rates per 1000 person-years were pooled for periods in and out of treatment, giving unadjusted out-of-treatment versus in-treatment rate ratios and differences; meta-regression by cohort characteristics; and, in recent cohorts reporting time intervals, rates in the first four weeks after starting or leaving treatment and afterwards, with a spline time-trend analysis. People in prison or recently released, untreated people and people in detoxification or other treatments were excluded.
can_establish: That across these cohorts death rates from all causes and from overdose were consistently lower during periods in methadone treatment than during periods out of it, and that all-cause mortality was highest in the first weeks after leaving methadone treatment (and, in two cohorts, buprenorphine treatment).
cannot_establish: That treatment caused the lower mortality or that leaving caused the higher mortality (all pooled estimates are unadjusted, and people leave and re-enter treatment non-randomly); why people died after leaving (no data on tolerance or drug use after leaving, and overdose data by time interval come from only three methadone cohorts and one buprenorphine cohort); or the risk of stopping opioids outside treatment (detoxification and untreated people were excluded).

sample.recruitment: Medline, Embase, PsycINFO and LILACS searched to September 2016 without language restrictions, plus the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, reference lists, PubMed related citations, online technical reports and monographs, and experts (p. 2, Methods › Search strategy and inclusion criteria, 1st paragraph). 2033 distinct records, 328 full texts assessed, 20 articles on 19 cohorts included (p. 3; Fig 1, p. 4). Cohort sizes range from 56 to 32,322 participants (Table 2, p. 6).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: cohort studies of people with opioid dependence with follow-up during and after methadone or buprenorphine maintenance and data to compute death rates in and out of treatment. Excluded: no human data; not original research; designs other than observational cohorts; not focused on opioid dependence; people in prison or recently released; treatment unknown or other than methadone or buprenorphine maintenance (methadone detoxification, antagonist therapy, therapeutic community); no all-cause or overdose deaths; insufficient data (p. 2). Untreated participants and those in other treatments were removed from the cohorts' data (Table 2 footnote, p. 6).
sample.demographics: Table 1 (p. 5): men 50.0% to 80.0% of each cohort with data; mean baseline age 23.4 to 39.6 years; four cohorts enrolled only people who inject opioids, two of them only people with HIV; non-opioid drug use, HIV and psychiatric and medical comorbidity mostly not available. Average methadone dose 47 to 116 mg/day and buprenorphine 10 to 12 mg/day where reported; addiction specialists provided treatment in 11 cohorts and general practitioners or mixed staff in 8 (p. 4; Table 2, p. 6).
sample.attrition: Loss to follow-up above 10% in four cohorts (up to 23.2%); complete ascertainment assumed for cohorts based on population mortality registers (Table 2, p. 6).
sample.selection_effects: Cohorts of people who entered maintenance treatment in high-income countries; never-treated people, people in detoxification or other treatments, and people in prison or recently released are excluded. Within cohorts, periods out of treatment follow non-random exits (dropping out, discharge), and the authors note that people lost to follow-up may be at higher risk of death (p. 12). For buprenorphine, 96% of deaths and 98% of person-years come from two Australian studies (p. 9).

exposure.measurement: Treatment status (in or out of methadone or buprenorphine maintenance) from cohort records; person-years in and out of treatment taken from the reports or derived from summary statistics on follow-up and retention (p. 3, Statistical analysis). Substitution medicines obtained illicitly were not captured, and a delayed record of leaving could misclassify some out-of-treatment deaths as in-treatment deaths (p. 12).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Average daily dose 47 to 116 mg methadone and 10 to 12 mg buprenorphine where reported; average follow-up 1.3 to 13.9 years (methadone) and 1.1 to 4.5 years (buprenorphine) (Table 2, p. 6). Treatment doses are cohort descriptors, not study conditions.
exposure.polysubstance: Recorded as a cohort characteristic but mostly not available (Table 1); all but four cohorts included people using non-opioid drugs (p. 3); not adjusted for in the pooled estimates.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. Whether people used opioids after leaving treatment was not known.

comparison.controls: Within-cohort comparison of person-time out of treatment (after leaving) with person-time in treatment; in the interval analyses, the first four weeks after starting or leaving against the remaining time (the first two weeks in Degenhardt et al., 2009, and Buster et al., 2002).
comparison.matching: None; the same people contribute both kinds of person-time; crude rates.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Reasons for leaving, drug use and tolerance after leaving, imprisonment and other time-varying factors were not available; patient characteristics were few and mostly measured at baseline (Tables 1–2; p. 11).

outcomes.instruments: All-cause and overdose deaths with person-years at risk, from cohort records and population mortality registers; rates per 1000 person-years with exact Poisson 95% intervals (p. 3).
outcomes.validity_norms: Overdose definitions and cause-of-death coding varied; the authors expect misclassification to underestimate overdose deaths (p. 12). Study quality was scored with a form built from the SIGN cohort checklist and an NDARC checklist (0 to 16; median 8, range 3 to 13; pp. 2 and 4; the form is in appendix 3, not read).
outcomes.operationalization: All-cause and overdose death rates in and out of treatment; unadjusted out-to-in rate ratios and rate differences from bivariate random-effects models on log rates; rates in the first four weeks after starting or leaving treatment and afterwards.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Two outcomes, two medicines, overall and interval comparisons, nine single-predictor meta-regressions per outcome and a trend analysis were reported without correction.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported (largely not applicable to register deaths).

analysis.effect_sizes: Methadone, all causes (16 cohorts): 11.3 (95% CI 8.4 to 15.2) deaths per 1000 person-years in treatment vs 36.1 (24.5 to 53.3) out; rate difference 24.9 (13.6 to 36.1); rate ratio 3.20 (2.65 to 3.86); I²=98%; leaving out one cohort at a time, 10.6–11.9 in and 32.5–39.1 out (p. 4; Fig 2, p. 7). Buprenorphine, all causes (3 cohorts): 4.3 (2.1 to 8.9) vs 9.5 (3.9 to 23.4); difference 5.2 (−1.0 to 11.4); ratio 2.20 (1.34 to 3.61). Methadone, overdose (11 cohorts): 2.6 (2.1 to 3.3) vs 12.7 (6.9 to 23.4); difference 10.0 (2.6 to 17.4); ratio 4.80 (2.90 to 7.96); I²=66% in and 97% out of treatment (p. 4; Fig 3, p. 10). Buprenorphine, overdose (1 cohort): 1.4 (1.0 to 2.0) vs 4.6 (3.9 to 5.4). Methadone intervals (5 cohorts): first four weeks of treatment 11.4 (5.8 to 22.4) vs 5.8 (5.0 to 6.7) later, difference 5.6 (−2.4 to 13.6), ratio 1.97 (0.94 to 4.10); first four weeks after leaving 32.1 (19.1 to 53.9) vs 13.5 (11.9 to 15.3) later, difference 18.6 (2.9 to 34.3), ratio 2.38 (1.51 to 3.74) (p. 5; Fig 4, p. 10). Trend analysis: fitted rate falling from 37.4 to 6.4 over the first four weeks of methadone treatment; 24.1 to 35.2 over the first two weeks after leaving, then declining (non-linearity P=0.04; p. 5; Fig 5, p. 11). Buprenorphine intervals (2 cohorts): 4.5 in both treatment periods; after leaving, 32.0 (13.2 to 77.5) vs 10.9 (8.5 to 13.9), difference 21.2 (−5.9 to 48.2), ratio 2.94 (1.34 to 6.46). Overdose intervals: methadone (3 cohorts) 3.5 (1.3 to 9.5) vs 2.0 (1.5 to 2.7) in treatment and 4.2 (1.8 to 9.9) vs 3.4 (2.3 to 5.1) out; buprenorphine (1 cohort) 0.9 vs 1.5 in and 10.8 vs 4.2 out (p. 5; Fig 6, p. 11). Editors' calculations from the printed per-cohort data: the random-effects pooled all-cause rates are close to the geometric means of the cohort rates (11.7 in, 36.2 out), so they describe an average cohort rather than an average person; person-time-weighted crude rates are 7.1 vs 16.4 per 1000 person-years for all causes (ratio 2.3) and 2.1 vs 5.8 for overdose (ratio 2.8).
analysis.covariates: None in the pooled estimates (crude rates). Nine cohort characteristics were examined one at a time by meta-regression (location, injecting, sex, age, methadone dose, inpatient induction, provider, follow-up period, loss to follow-up; Table 3, p. 8). Five methadone cohorts and one buprenorphine cohort reported adjusted rate ratios (Table 4, p. 9).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the PRISMA statement was followed and the exclusion criteria are described as prespecified (p. 2).
analysis.selective_reporting: The planned estimates appear to be reported. The summary box and discussion stress a high-risk induction period although the interval comparison for the first four weeks of methadone treatment was not statistically significant; overdose data by time interval exist for only three methadone cohorts.
analysis.power: Not addressed. The buprenorphine estimates rest on three cohorts dominated by one, and the methadone overdose estimate for the first four weeks after leaving on 20 deaths (editors' count from Fig 6).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Consistently lower crude death rates in than out of methadone treatment across 16 cohorts (pooled ratios 3.2 for all causes and 4.8 for overdose, with very high heterogeneity); a peak in all-cause mortality in the first four weeks after leaving methadone treatment (32.1 vs 13.5 per 1000 person-years later); weaker and sparser evidence for buprenorphine (three cohorts, two Australian).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract's conclusions are hedged: retention is associated with lower mortality, and confounding and selection bias still need to be addressed (p. 1). Elsewhere the paper goes further. The summary box says mortality in treatment is less than a third of that "expected in the absence of opioid substitution treatment" (p. 1), a counterfactual that a comparison of periods after non-random exits does not provide, and the implications state that methadone and probably buprenorphine reduce mortality (p. 12). The abstract and box present the start of methadone treatment as a period of particularly increased risk, but the interval comparison was not significant (ratio 1.97, 0.94 to 4.10) and the steep early fall in the trend analysis is anchored by one cohort (Degenhardt et al., 2009: 37.5 per 1000 person-years in the first two weeks, against 4.4 to 15.1 in the first four weeks in the other cohorts). The abstract says overdose mortality evolved similarly, but the three methadone cohorts with interval data show no clear overdose peak after leaving (4.2 vs 3.4). The headline of 25 fewer deaths per 1000 person-years is an average across cohorts; the three largest, recent register cohorts show differences of 5.5 to 11.2. The discussion's statement that buprenorphine mortality was significantly lower than methadone mortality in both periods (p. 9) has no test or estimate in the results.

timeline.event: Gearing & Schweitzer: earliest included methadone cohort (New York, follow-up 1965–72).

Degenhardt et al.: largest included methadone cohort (New South Wales, 31,846 participants), with the highest rate in the first two weeks of treatment (37.5 per 1000 person-years) and 20.0 in the first two weeks after leaving.

Degenhardt et al.: earlier systematic review and meta-analysis of mortality among people who use heroin and other opioids regularly or dependently, cited for a larger effect of treatment on overdose than on other deaths (ref. 11).

Kimber et al.: New South Wales cohort covering both medicines (26,064 methadone and 11,940 buprenorphine participants), the source of 87% of the buprenorphine deaths in this review; its sensitivity simulation suggested that the lower mortality with buprenorphine than with methadone during the first four weeks of treatment was unlikely to be caused by unmeasured confounding (as cited, p. 11).
Cousins et al.: Irish national methadone cohort, with a commentary by Hickman, Macleod and Degenhardt on accumulating evidence about mortality on and off substitution treatment (refs 12 and 37).
This review.

replication.where_it_stands: The standard pooled estimate of mortality in and out of opioid substitution treatment, built on crude comparisons within cohorts. Its direction (lower mortality in treatment; a high-risk period after leaving) is the same in all 16 methadone cohorts; its magnitudes are unadjusted averages across very heterogeneous cohorts and are larger than in the big recent register cohorts. The buprenorphine estimates rest essentially on one Australian cohort.

funding.affiliations_note: Two authors (Wiessing, Ferri) work at the EMCDDA, a co-funder. Degenhardt is an author of two included cohorts that contribute much of the person-time (Degenhardt et al., 2009; Kimber et al., 2015; refs 6 and 10), of the earlier review (ref. 11) and of the commentary cited (ref. 12). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: Individual-level register cohorts from several countries, including low- and middle-income countries, recording every treatment entry and exit with the reason for leaving, imprisonment, and time-varying confounders at each transition, with overdose and other causes of death by week since starting and leaving, analysed with methods for time-varying confounding and informative censoring (for example marginal structural models, as the authors suggest), and comparing methadone and buprenorphine within the same cohorts.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (people with opioid dependence), exposure (periods in methadone or buprenorphine maintenance), comparator (periods out of treatment) and outcomes (all-cause and overdose mortality) are stated.
No protocol or registration is mentioned; only the exclusion criteria are described as prespecified.
The restriction to cohort studies is explained: long-term trials comparing the medicines on mortality are hardly feasible, and cohorts capture mortality in and out of treatment (pp. 1–2).

Four databases to September 2016 (about six months before acceptance), no language limits, the full strategy in appendix 1 (not read), reference lists, related citations, technical reports and monographs, and experts; study registries are not mentioned.
Two investigators independently reviewed titles, abstracts and full texts, with disagreements resolved by consensus with a third (p. 2).
Two independent reviewers extracted the data (abstract; p. 2; contributors, p. 13).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Fig 1 gives the 308 excluded full texts as counts by reason, but no list of excluded studies; the online appendices are titled searches, supplementary tables A and B, and quality score.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Tables 1–2 give location, population, injecting, HIV, comorbidity, sex, age, size, dose, induction, provider, follow-up period and length, loss to follow-up, outcomes and quality score; many cells are 'not available', and how each cohort defined leaving treatment (the comparator) is not described.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: A purpose-built 0–16 score drawn from the SIGN cohort checklist and an NDARC checklist, covering external and internal validity and biases relevant to cohort studies, with scores per study (Table 2); whether it assesses confounding and selection bias explicitly can be judged only from appendix 3, which was not read.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

Bivariate random-effects models on log rates (REML), allowing for the correlation between in- and out-of-treatment rates, with sensitivity analyses for within-cohort correlation. Crude rates were pooled and every estimate is labelled unadjusted; the adjusted ratios available from six cohorts are shown separately (Table 4) and were not smaller.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: The quality score was not used in meta-regression or sensitivity analyses; only leave-one-out analyses were done.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Confounding, non-random exits, informative censoring and misclassification are discussed at length, and the conclusions call for research that accounts for confounding and selection bias (pp. 11–12; abstract).
Heterogeneity is quantified (I² 66% to 98%) and explored with nine cohort characteristics; the injecting/HIV and provider associations are reported and discussed.
Extended Egger test: some small-study effect for all-cause mortality (P=0.05), attributed to small cohorts of people with HIV who inject; none for overdose (P=0.14) (p. 4).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and competing interests are declared (p. 13).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 9 depends on appendix 3, which was not read, but it cannot change the rating. Two critical items are not met (no protocol, item 2; no list of excluded studies, item 7), which under AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence in the review as a synthesis. Searching, duplicate selection and extraction, the statistical model and the discussion of bias are otherwise strong. The low rating concerns the review's completeness and reproducibility more than its arithmetic: the per-cohort data are printed in full (Figs 2–4 and 6) and every methadone cohort shows higher mortality out of treatment. The pooled figures are unadjusted averages across very heterogeneous cohorts and should be cited as associations, with the range in the large cohorts beside them.

key_findings.finding: The review included 19 cohorts (20 articles published 1974–2016; 11 from Europe/Israel, 4 from North America, 4 from Australia): 18 methadone cohorts with 122,885 participants followed between 1965 and 2010 and 3 buprenorphine cohorts with 15,831 participants followed between 1990 and 2010; average follow-up 1.3 to 13.9 years (methadone) and 1.1 to 4.5 years (buprenorphine).
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. 1); Results › Study characteristics, 1st paragraph (begins p. 3) and 2nd paragraph (p. 4); Tables 1–2 (pp. 5–6)

key_findings.finding: Methadone, all causes: pooled 11.3 (95% CI 8.4 to 15.2) deaths per 1000 person-years in treatment vs 36.1 (24.5 to 53.3) out of treatment; unadjusted rate difference 24.9 (13.6 to 36.1) per 1000 person-years and rate ratio 3.20 (2.65 to 3.86); 16 cohorts; I²=98%.
key_findings.locator: Results › All cause mortality during and after opioid substitution treatment, 1st paragraph; Fig 2 (p. 7)

key_findings.finding: In every one of the 16 methadone cohorts the all-cause death rate was higher out of treatment than in treatment; cohort rates ranged from 5.1 to 39.5 per 1000 person-years in treatment and from 12.4 to 130.2 out of treatment.
key_findings.locator: Fig 2 (per-cohort rates)
key_findings.note: Editors' reading of the printed per-cohort rates.

key_findings.finding: Buprenorphine, all causes (3 cohorts): 4.3 (2.1 to 8.9) deaths per 1000 person-years in treatment vs 9.5 (3.9 to 23.4) out; unadjusted rate difference 5.2 (−1.0 to 11.4), rate ratio 2.20 (1.34 to 3.61).
key_findings.locator: Results › All cause mortality during and after opioid substitution treatment, 2nd paragraph; Fig 2 (p. 7)
key_findings.note: The difference interval includes zero while the ratio interval excludes 1; the discussion calls the in–out disparity for buprenorphine not significant (p. 9).

key_findings.finding: Methadone, overdose (11 cohorts): 2.6 (2.1 to 3.3) deaths per 1000 person-years in treatment vs 12.7 (6.9 to 23.4) out; unadjusted rate difference 10.0 (2.6 to 17.4), rate ratio 4.80 (2.90 to 7.96); heterogeneity I²=66% in treatment and 97% out. Buprenorphine (1 cohort): 1.4 vs 4.6.
key_findings.locator: Results › Overdose mortality during and after opioid substitution treatment, 1st paragraph; Fig 3 (p. 10)

key_findings.finding: Out-of-treatment overdose rates were higher in methadone cohorts treated by specialists than in those treated by general practitioners or mixed staff: 20.8 (11.1 to 38.8) vs 5.6 (2.5 to 12.5) per 1000 person-years (P=0.01, likelihood-ratio test of in- and out-of-treatment rates together). All-cause rates were higher in the four cohorts made up entirely of people who inject opioids: 23.4 in and 109.9 out of treatment, against 9.0 and 25.8 (P=0.001, same test). Location, sex, age, methadone dose, inpatient induction, follow-up period and loss to follow-up were not significantly associated with the rates.
key_findings.locator: Table 3; also p. 4, Results › All cause mortality…, 1st paragraph, and Overdose mortality…, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: In the first four weeks after leaving methadone treatment (5 cohorts), all-cause mortality was 32.1 (19.1 to 53.9) per 1000 person-years, against 13.5 (11.9 to 15.3) later out of treatment; difference 18.6 (2.9 to 34.3), ratio 2.38 (1.51 to 3.74).
key_findings.locator: Results › All cause mortality by time interval in and out of treatment, 1st paragraph; Fig 4 (p. 10)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: 32.1 is about 5.5 times the pooled rate after the first four weeks in treatment (5.8); ratio of two separately pooled rates, without an interval.

key_findings.finding: In the first four weeks of methadone treatment, all-cause mortality was 11.4 (5.8 to 22.4) per 1000 person-years, against 5.8 (5.0 to 6.7) for the rest of treatment; difference 5.6 (−2.4 to 13.6), ratio 1.97 (0.94 to 4.10), not statistically significant. The first-period rate was 4.4 to 15.1 in four cohorts and 37.5 in the first two weeks in Degenhardt et al. (2009).
key_findings.locator: Results › All cause mortality by time interval in and out of treatment, 1st paragraph; Fig 4 (p. 10)

key_findings.finding: In the trend analysis, the fitted all-cause rate fell from 37.4 to 6.4 per 1000 person-years over the first four weeks of methadone treatment and was fairly stable afterwards; after leaving, it stayed between 24.1 and 35.2 during the first two weeks and then declined progressively (non-linearity P=0.04).
key_findings.locator: Results › All cause mortality by time interval in and out of treatment, 2nd paragraph; Fig 5 (p. 11)

key_findings.finding: Buprenorphine time intervals (2 cohorts): 4.5 deaths per 1000 person-years both in the first four weeks and later in treatment; after leaving, 32.0 (13.2 to 77.5) in the first four weeks vs 10.9 (8.5 to 13.9) later; difference 21.2 (−5.9 to 48.2), ratio 2.94 (1.34 to 6.46).
key_findings.locator: Results › All cause mortality by time interval in and out of treatment, 3rd paragraph; Fig 4 (p. 10)

key_findings.finding: Overdose by time interval: in three methadone cohorts, 3.5 (1.3 to 9.5) overdose deaths per 1000 person-years in the first four weeks vs 2.0 (1.5 to 2.7) later in treatment, and 4.2 (1.8 to 9.9) in the first four weeks vs 3.4 (2.3 to 5.1) later out of treatment; in the one buprenorphine cohort, 0.9 vs 1.5 in treatment and 10.8 vs 4.2 out of treatment.
key_findings.locator: Results › Overdose mortality by time interval in and out of treatment (one paragraph); Fig 6 (p. 11)
key_findings.note: The methadone estimate for the first period after leaving rests on 20 overdose deaths (editors' count from Fig 6).

key_findings.finding: Where cohorts reported adjusted estimates (five methadone, one buprenorphine), adjustment to various degrees for demographics, severity of drug use, treatment and comorbidity (Degenhardt 2009 only for age, sex and calendar year) left the all-cause out-to-in ratios unchanged in two methadone cohorts and 15.5% to 35.5% larger in three, and 16.8% larger in the buprenorphine cohort; overdose ratios were unchanged in three methadone cohorts and 25.8% and 28.6% larger in two, Evans 2015 and Nosyk 2015, whose overdose ratios combine maintenance with detoxification or include never-treated participants (Table 4 footnote). [page: pp. 4, 9]
key_findings.locator: Results › All cause mortality…, 4th paragraph; Overdose mortality…, 2nd paragraph; Table 4 (p. 9)

key_findings.finding: Some evidence of small-study effects for all-cause mortality (P=0.05), with higher rates in small cohorts mostly of people with HIV who inject; none for overdose (P=0.14). Removing any one cohort left the pooled methadone rates at 10.6–11.9 in and 32.5–39.1 out of treatment for all causes, and 2.4–2.8 and 10.6–14.9 for overdose.
key_findings.locator: Results › All cause mortality…, 3rd paragraph; Overdose mortality…, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors note that methadone's long half-life could contribute to deaths in the first three to four days after leaving, but suggest that the excess across the first four weeks could be explained by loss of tolerance to the toxic effects of heroin, assuming many people return to use, and probably by use of several substances; they note similar peaks after prison release and hospital discharge and more deaths from suicide and injury in that period. No data on tolerance or drug use after leaving were available to the review.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Mortality risk during specific periods in and out of methadone treatment, 3rd paragraph ('Although the long half life…', right column)

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: people leave and re-enter treatment non-randomly, so confounding may be large; people lost to follow-up may be at higher risk (informative censoring); the amount and direction of the resulting bias in the pooled estimates is hard to assess; overdose deaths when substitution medicines were obtained illicitly were not captured; delayed records of leaving could misclassify deaths; overdose definitions and coding varied; all studies came from high-income countries.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Strengths and limitations, 2nd paragraph (begins p. 11) to 4th paragraph (p. 12)

key_findings.finding: For buprenorphine, 96% of the included deaths and 98% of person-years came from Australian studies, 87% and 86% from the study by Kimber and colleagues.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Mortality risk during specific periods in and out of buprenorphine treatment (one paragraph)
key_findings.note: From Fig 2 the Kimber share of buprenorphine person-years is 84.8% (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Editors' calculations from the printed per-cohort rates: in the three largest methadone cohorts (Degenhardt 2009, Evans 2015, Kimber 2015; 83% of all-cause person-years) the out-minus-in differences were 8.5, 11.2 and 5.5 deaths per 1000 person-years (ratios 2.5, 2.7 and 1.8); in the three largest overdose cohorts (Kimber 2015, Buster 2002, Cousins 2016; 82% of overdose person-years) out-of-treatment overdose rates were 4.8, 2.4 and 3.8 against 1.8, 2.2 and 2.4 in treatment.
key_findings.locator: Fig 2 (p. 7); Fig 3 (p. 10)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation, not reported by the authors; it shows that the pooled differences describe an average cohort and are larger than in the big recent register cohorts.

reporting_issues.issue: Average methadone follow-up is given as 1.3 to 13.9 years in the abstract, results and Table 2, but as 1.3 to 15.8 years in the limitations.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; Table 2 supports 13.9.

reporting_issues.issue: The results say that more than 70% of participants were men; from Tables 1–2 the participant-weighted share is about 67% (editors' calculation; two cohorts lack data), 70.5% is the unweighted mean of cohort percentages, and 8 of the 16 methadone cohorts with data are below 70%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the cohort range (50% to 80% men), not 'more than 70% of participants'.

reporting_issues.issue: Significance is judged inconsistently for buprenorphine: the in–out comparison (difference −1.0 to 11.4; ratio 1.34 to 3.61) is called not significant, while the comparison after leaving, with the same pattern (difference −5.9 to 48.2; ratio 1.34 to 6.46), is called significantly increased.
reporting_issues.consequence: Both buprenorphine comparisons should be described as uncertain in absolute terms.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion states that mortality was significantly lower with buprenorphine than with methadone both in and out of treatment, but no such comparison, test or estimate appears in the results, tables or figures; it would compare 3 buprenorphine cohorts with 16 methadone cohorts from different countries and periods.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not citable as a finding of this review.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion says that only two cohorts reported overdose data specifically (refs 7 and 10), whereas the results and Fig 6 use three methadone cohorts with overdose data by time interval (including Cousins et al., 2016).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; either way the overdose evidence by time interval is thin.

reporting_issues.issue: Three of the unadjusted rate ratios in Table 4 differ from the crude ratios implied by Figs 2-3: Degenhardt 2009, all causes, 1.91 (Fig 2: 14.3/5.8 = 2.5); Nosyk 2015, all causes, 3.04 (130.2/22.4 = 5.8); Buster 2002, overdose, 0.87 (Fig 3: 2.4/2.2 = 1.1). The Table 4 footnote explains only the overdose ratios of Evans 2015 (maintenance combined with detoxification) and Nosyk 2015 (never-treated participants included), neither of which is in Fig 3; the three differences are not explained.
reporting_issues.consequence: The percentage changes after adjustment refer to the primary studies' own models, which for some cohorts used other person-time than the pooled data.

reporting_issues.issue: Cross-reference slips: the study by Kimber and colleagues is cited as ref. 13 (the PRISMA statement) instead of ref. 10 (p. 9); adjustment results are attributed to Table 3 instead of Table 4 (p. 12); the Kimber share of buprenorphine person-years is printed as 86%, while Fig 2 gives 84.8%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; no effect on the estimates.

reporting_issues.issue: The summary box states 25 fewer deaths per 1000 person-years in methadone treatment and a rate in treatment less than a third of that expected without treatment; both rest on unadjusted random-effects averages across cohorts, and the counterfactual wording is not supported by a comparison of periods after non-random exits.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should say 'associated with', give the range in the large cohorts and avoid 'expected without treatment'.

design_detail: Narrative review (journal section Review) by three authors arguing, from the receptor evidence, against fixed limits on buprenorphine doses and on their reimbursement. Its Methods section explains how mu-opioid receptor (µOR) availability is measured ([11C]-carfentanil PET; a pharmacological model) and the limits of those studies, but states no search, dates or selection criteria. The evidence reviewed is the authors' own: three PET studies in people dependent on heroin who were not seeking treatment (Zubieta et al., 2000, n=3; Greenwald et al., 2003, n=5; Greenwald et al., 2007, n=10) and one self-administration study with modelled receptor estimates (Comer et al., 2005, 7 maintained and 8 placebo-maintained volunteers), re-analysed with curve fits that estimate availability at doses and times not studied (Table 1; Figs. 1–3). Read from the corrected proof (article in press).
can_establish: How, in the authors' small inpatient studies of people dependent on heroin who were not in treatment, buprenorphine dose and time since the last dose related to brain µOR availability, plasma levels, withdrawal and responses to heroin or hydromorphone, and which availability thresholds the authors infer from these data.
cannot_establish: Whether the availability figures and thresholds hold for people in treatment, women, people with other substance use or with mental or physical illness, or people who use fentanyl or opioids other than heroin and hydromorphone (none were studied), how precise they are (3 to 10 people per PET study, no intervals, curve fits for doses and hours not studied), or whether any dose policy improves outcomes (no outcome data are reviewed).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). The PET studies reviewed enrolled people dependent on heroin who were not seeking treatment and who were studied during inpatient stays (2.2.2, 1st paragraph, PDF p. 3).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No selection criteria stated for the review. The PET studies reviewed admitted ages 18–50 and excluded non-opioid substance use disorders other than nicotine, depressive, psychotic and anxiety disorders, pregnancy, and medical conditions such as active hepatitis, respiratory or neurological disease (2.2.2, 2nd–4th paragraphs, PDF p. 3).
sample.demographics: Not tabulated. Many fewer women than men took part in the PET studies (2.2.2, 2nd paragraph, PDF p. 3); the preliminary study enrolled men only, as its title in the reference list says (Zubieta et al., 2000; PDF p. 11). Numbers per study: 3 (Zubieta et al., 2000), 5 (Greenwald et al., 2003), 10 (Greenwald et al., 2007: 5 heavier and 5 lighter smokers), 7 maintained against 8 placebo-maintained (Comer et al., 2005) (Results, PDF pp. 4–5; Table 1; Fig. 4 legend, PDF p. 7).
sample.selection_effects: The authors chose the evidence, and all of the receptor and blockade data come from their own studies: Greenwald is first author of the 2003 and 2007 PET studies and a co-author of Zubieta et al. (2000), and Comer is first author of the 2005 study (reference list, PDF pp. 9–11). The participants were relatively healthy people dependent on heroin, not in treatment, who kept using opioids between inpatient stays; the authors state that they do not represent patients in clinical practice and that generalizability to people dependent on other opioids, such as oxycodone or hydrocodone, is unclear (2.2.2, PDF p. 3). All imaging used one branded buprenorphine-only tablet (2.2.3, 7th paragraph, PDF p. 4).

exposure.measurement: Buprenorphine given by the investigators under double-blind or controlled inpatient conditions: a sublingual liquid in Zubieta et al. (2000; a formulation discontinued before FDA approval), buprenorphine-only sublingual tablets in the Greenwald studies, buprenorphine/naloxone sublingual tablets in Comer et al. (2005); plasma buprenorphine and norbuprenorphine measured in the Greenwald studies (Results, 1st–5th paragraphs, PDF p. 4).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only. Zubieta et al. (2000): 2, 16 and 0 mg/day. Greenwald et al. (2003): 32, 16, 2 and 0 mg/day for 12 days each, scans 4 h after the dose. Greenwald et al. (2007): 16 mg/day for at least 14 days, then double-blind placebo with scans 4, 28, 52 and 76 h after the last dose. Comer et al. (2005): buprenorphine/naloxone 2/0.5, 8/2 and 32/8 mg/day for 14 days each, tested 15 h after the dose. Challenge opioids given by the investigators: intranasal heroin 0–100 mg (Comer et al., 2005) and hydromorphone 24 mg intramuscularly (Greenwald et al., 2003 and 2007) (Results, PDF p. 4; Table 1, PDF p. 5).
exposure.polysubstance: People with non-opioid substance use disorders other than nicotine were excluded (2.2.2, PDF p. 3). Acute nicotine deprivation was required before every scan, and heavier smokers (≥20 cigarettes/day) had lower µOR availability than lighter smokers (≤15/day) in Greenwald et al. (2007) (Results, 8th paragraph, PDF pp. 5 and 7; Fig. 4). Participants kept using opioids (by urinalysis) during outpatient periods between inpatient stays (Results, 3rd paragraph, PDF p. 4).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Zubieta et al. (2000): admitted to an inpatient unit 4 days before each scan, with daily urine testing; Greenwald et al. (2003): a 12-day placebo period as the baseline (Results, 1st–2nd paragraphs, PDF p. 4).

comparison.controls: Within-person placebo (0 mg) in Zubieta et al. (2000) and Greenwald et al. (2003). Greenwald et al. (2007) expressed availability against the placebo condition of the 2003 study, that is, against other people; Comer et al. (2005) compared 7 maintained volunteers with a separate group of 8 heroin-detoxified volunteers on placebo (Results, PDF p. 4; Table 1, notes a and c, PDF p. 5).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Within-person dose comparisons need no premorbid data, but the between-group references (Greenwald et al., 2007, against the 2003 placebo condition; Comer's separate placebo group) assume comparable receptor availability in different people; the authors warn that absolute levels should therefore be read cautiously (Table 1, note c, PDF p. 5).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not described for the placebo conditions.

outcomes.instruments: [11C]-carfentanil PET: µOR availability as non-displaceable binding potential (distribution volume ratio against occipital cortex) in up to seven regions (prefrontal BA 10, anterior cingulate BA 25 and BA 32, caudate, thalamus, nucleus accumbens, amygdala), expressed as percent of placebo; earliest scan 4 h after the dose (2.1.1, PDF p. 3). Comer et al. (2005): receptor availability not imaged but estimated with a pharmacological model from heroin self-administration and ratings of “good drug effect”, “high” and “potent” (2.1.2, PDF p. 3; Table 1, note a). Ratings of withdrawal, agonist symptoms and craving; responses to hydromorphone and heroin challenges.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors avoid the word occupancy: it cannot be measured directly in humans, and a fall in availability equals a rise in occupancy only if receptor affinity and endogenous opioid levels stay constant (2.1.1, 1st paragraph, PDF p. 3). They state that there is no gold-standard definition of clinically meaningful blockade and that the availability needed for withdrawal suppression or for blockade is not known (2.2.1, 1st paragraph, PDF p. 3).
outcomes.operationalization: Blockade is defined by the authors as no reactivity to an opioid (physiological effects or subjective effects linked to liking) and no responding for it (reinforcing effects), compared statistically with placebo; they hold that clinicians and policymakers expect this in most patients, not only in some (4.2.1, 3rd paragraph, PDF p. 8).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no new statistical synthesis); the re-analyses report no tests or intervals.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind dosing is reported for Zubieta et al. (2000) and for the placebo substitution in Greenwald et al. (2007); blinding of image analysis is not reported (Results, PDF p. 4).

analysis.effect_sizes: No confidence intervals or test statistics are printed for any estimate. µOR availability against placebo, 4 h after the daily dose: Zubieta et al. (2000, n=3) 50% (hypothalamus) to 64% (cerebellum) at 2 mg/day and 5% (hypothalamus) to 21% (thalamus) at 16 mg/day (Results, 1st paragraph, PDF p. 4); Greenwald et al. (2003, n=5), range of regional means, 53–72% at 2 mg/day, 9–20% at 16 mg/day and 2–12% at 32 mg/day, with curve-fit estimates for doses not studied of 71–85% (1 mg), 36–55% (4 mg), 20–35% (8 mg), 13–24% (12 mg) and 4–15% (24 mg) (Table 1, PDF p. 5). Comer et al. (2005), modelled availability 15 h after the dose: 21–31% (2/0.5 mg), 11–22% (8/2 mg), 6–12% (32/8 mg), with heroin 50 and 100 mg self-administration only modestly reduced (Results, 4th paragraph, PDF p. 4; Table 1). After stopping 16 mg/day (Greenwald et al., 2007, n=10): against the 2003 placebo condition 27–31% at 4 h, 54–61% at 28 h, 65–75% at 52 h and 77–94% at 76 h (Table 1); adjusted to the 2003 4-h value, estimated 13–25% at 4 h, 37–46% at 24 h, 56–73% at 48 h and 75–90% at 72 h (Results, 6th paragraph, PDF pp. 4–5); hydromorphone's subjective effects significantly smaller at 4 and 28 h than at 52 and 76 h (Results, 5th paragraph, PDF p. 4). Between-person variation at 16 and 32 mg/day (coefficients of variation): 24% and 21% for availability, 39% and 54% for plasma levels, 129% and 109% for withdrawal symptoms (2.2.3, 8th paragraph, PDF p. 4); 3.5-fold range of availability at 2 mg/day in most regions (4.1, 3rd paragraph, PDF p. 7).
analysis.preregistration_detail: A narrative review; no protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection of the authors' own studies. The re-analysed estimates (curve fits, Table 1 values for doses not studied, hourly values after stopping) are printed without intervals or tests, and individual values are shown only in Figs. 2 and 4. The abstract gives the availability thresholds without the qualifiers of the Summary (preliminary modelling; blockade not reliably observed).
analysis.power: Not applicable. The authors note that the small samples left too little power to examine sex or age (2.2.2, 2nd paragraph, PDF p. 3) and prevent firm conclusions about nicotine (Results, 8th paragraph, PDF p. 7).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 3, 5 and 10 people dependent on heroin who were not in treatment, buprenorphine lowered µOR availability with dose (to about 9–20% of placebo at 16 mg/day and 2–12% at 32 mg/day, 4 h after the dose); availability rose again over the 3 days after stopping 16 mg/day, while hydromorphone's effects returned in part; responses to heroin and hydromorphone were reduced but not abolished at the highest doses studied, and opioid use continued between inpatient stays. Availability thresholds for withdrawal suppression and for blockade are inferred from curve fits across these small studies.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract presents the thresholds (50% or less for withdrawal suppression, below 20% for blockade of typical doses, below 10% against higher doses) as results and translates them into single daily doses for most patients (abstract, PDF p. 1). The body says that neither threshold is known (2.2.1, PDF p. 3), that blockade “has not been reliably observed” under the doses studied, and that the 20% figure rests on preliminary modelling (4.3 Summary, PDF p. 8); the data come from volunteers whom the authors call unrepresentative of patients in clinical practice (2.2.2, PDF p. 3). The conclusion that fixed dose limits and reimbursement limits are unwarranted is a policy argument resting on these estimates and on clinical-trial findings cited without appraisal (4.2, PDF pp. 7–8).

timeline.event: Preliminary PET study (Zubieta et al., 2000): 3 men dependent on heroin, liquid buprenorphine 2 and 16 mg/day against placebo, as described in this review.
Self-administration study (Greenwald et al., 2002): 16 mg/day and 32 mg every other day did not fully block the reinforcing effect of hydromorphone 24 mg intramuscularly, as described in this review.
Dose–response PET study (Greenwald et al., 2003): 5 volunteers, 0 to 32 mg/day, as described in this review.
Self-administration study with modelled receptor estimates (Comer et al., 2005): 7 maintained against 8 placebo-maintained volunteers, intranasal heroin, as described in this review.
Time-course PET study after stopping 16 mg/day (Greenwald et al., 2007): 10 volunteers, scans 4 to 76 h after the last dose, as described in this review.

A population pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic model for a subcutaneous depot formulation is said to extend these relationships (Nasser et al., 2014, with Greenwald as a co-author, as described, PDF p. 7).

replication.where_it_stands: The receptor-availability figures come from three small PET studies by one research group (18 participants in all) and one modelling study, all by the authors; no independent PET replication is described in the review. Whether they apply to people in treatment, to women, or to people who use fentanyl is not addressed by these data.

Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: PET studies of µOR availability with opioid challenges, in larger samples of people in buprenorphine treatment that include women, people with mental health and other substance use conditions and people who use fentanyl, scanned at several times across the dosing interval and after stopping, with pre-registered analyses and reported intervals; and randomized comparisons of dose policies on treatment outcomes.

domains.note: No search, databases, dates or criteria; the Methods describe measurement, not selection, and the evidence was chosen by the authors.

No formal appraisal, but the limits of the PET studies are set out at length (2.2, PDF p. 3: small samples, unrepresentative volunteers, scans from 4 h, between-group references); the clinical trials cited for higher doses are not appraised.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: All receptor and blockade data come from the authors' studies (Zubieta et al., 2000, with Greenwald; Greenwald et al., 2003 and 2007; Comer et al., 2005) and from the authors' re-analyses of them.

The body labels the thresholds as preliminary modelling and says the true thresholds are unknown, but the abstract states them, with dose translations, as results; the dose-policy section mixes evidence with advocacy.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against dose limits
domains.note: Reasons given for dose limits are presented only as misinterpretations; diversion is acknowledged in one paragraph; evidence that lower doses suffice for some people is mentioned but not weighed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated risk-of-bias instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). The review is candid about the methodological limits of its evidence, but its selection is unsystematic and its evidence is the authors' own small PET and laboratory studies, re-analysed by them. It may be cited for the receptor-availability figures and the time course after stopping, as the authors' summary of their own studies, with the numbers of participants, the doses and the scan times stated; it should not be cited for availability thresholds as established facts, for people who use fentanyl, or for dosing.

key_findings.finding: In the authors' summary of earlier human studies, buprenorphine brought on moderate to severe withdrawal in people maintained on methadone 60 mg/day, and less in people on methadone 25–30 mg/day or on heroin; citing animal and human studies, the review says that whether it precipitates withdrawal depends on the level of dependence, the opioid depended on, and the time since its last dose. (The dependence sentence is not limited to animal studies: it cites Kosten and Kleber, 1988, and Walsh et al., 1995a, human studies by their titles, as well as Sell et al., 2003, and Woods' animal work.)
key_findings.locator: 1.2.1 Pre-FDA approval, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand: summarized from cited studies (Kosten and Kleber, 1988; Kosten et al., 1991; Strain et al., 1992; Walsh et al., 1995a) that were not read.

key_findings.finding: Preliminary PET study (Zubieta et al., 2000; 3 volunteers dependent on heroin; scans 4 h after the daily dose): against placebo, µOR availability was 50% (hypothalamus) to 64% (cerebellum) at 2 mg/day and 5% (hypothalamus) to 21% (thalamus) at 16 mg/day; withdrawal and heroin-craving scores fell linearly with dose.
key_findings.locator: 3. Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Finding unchanged and confirmed; note corrected to: Availability is the share of receptors still free to bind the tracer; the authors treat a fall in availability as proportional to a rise in occupancy if receptor affinity and endogenous opioid levels are assumed constant (2.1.1, PDF p. 3). The legend of Fig. 1 gives 12–33% for 8 mg/day, against 20–35% in Table 1 (see reporting issues). (The source says 'proportional', under an assumption, not 'equate ... only if'.)
key_findings.locator: 3. Results, 2nd–3rd paragraphs (p. 4); Table 1 and note b (p. 5); Fig. 1, left panel (p. 5)
key_findings.note: Availability is the share of receptors still free to bind the tracer; the authors equate a fall in availability with a rise in occupancy only if receptor affinity and endogenous opioid levels are constant (2.1.1, PDF p. 3). The legend of Fig. 1 gives 12–33% for 8 mg/day, against 20–35% in Table 1 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Even at 32 mg/day, participants in the dose–response study kept using opioids (by urinalysis) during outpatient periods between inpatient stays; the authors say 32 mg/day did not fully deter opioid use in these volunteers, who were not in treatment.
key_findings.locator: 3. Results, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Self-administration study (Comer et al., 2005; 7 volunteers on buprenorphine/naloxone 2/0.5, 8/2 and 32/8 mg/day, 14 days each, tested 15 h after the dose, against 8 heroin-detoxified volunteers on placebo): self-administration of intranasal heroin 50 mg and 100 mg decreased only modestly when modelled receptor availability was 21%, 11% and 6% (Table 1 ranges 21–31%, 11–22% and 6–12%).
key_findings.locator: 3. Results, 4th paragraph (p. 4); Table 1 and note a (p. 5); Fig. 3, upper right (p. 6)
key_findings.note: Availability here is a model estimate from behaviour, not an image; the authors say it should not be compared with the PET values (4.1, 1st paragraph, PDF p. 7). Fig. 3 has control-group data for 12.5 and 50 mg only.

key_findings.finding: Time-course study (Greenwald et al., 2007; 10 volunteers stabilized on 16 mg/day, then double-blind placebo; measures 4, 28, 52 and 76 h after the last dose): µOR availability rose as plasma buprenorphine fell (an inverse exponential relation); the subjective effects of hydromorphone 24 mg intramuscularly were significantly reduced at 4 h and 28 h compared with 52 h and 76 h; near-zero availability was projected at plasma levels of about 14 ng/mL.
key_findings.locator: 3. Results, 5th paragraph
key_findings.note: No test statistics are printed. The 14 ng/mL projection comes from fits whose maximum plasma concentration was constrained to 15 ng/mL or less (Fig. 2 legend, PDF p. 6).

key_findings.finding: After the last 16 mg/day dose, µOR availability adjusted to the 2003 study's 4-h value was estimated at 13–25% across regions at 4 h, 19–30% at 8 h, 24–36% at 12 h, 29–41% at 16 h, 37–46% at 24 h, 56–73% at 48 h and 75–90% at 72 h; Table 1 gives the unadjusted values against the 2003 placebo condition as 27–31% at 4 h, 54–61% at 28 h, 65–75% at 52 h and 77–94% at 76 h.
key_findings.locator: 3. Results, 6th paragraph (starts p. 4; values on p. 5); Table 1, Greenwald et al. (2007) row and note c (p. 5); Fig. 1, right panel (p. 5)
key_findings.note: Scans were made at 4, 28, 52 and 76 h only; the values at 8, 12, 16, 24, 48 and 72 h are read from fitted curves. The two series differ because of the adjustment (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: The authors' re-analysis of Comer et al. (2005) suggests that nearly all receptors would need to be occupied, beyond what 32 mg/day achieved, to fully suppress self-administration of heroin at naturalistic doses; in the time-course study, the agonist response to hydromorphone recovered modestly with time since the last dose (loss of blockade).
key_findings.locator: 3. Results, 7th paragraph; Fig. 3 (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: Blockade was incomplete in the other studies cited: 16 mg/day did not fully block the reinforcing effect of intravenous heroin 12.5 mg and 25 mg, and 16 mg/day or 32 mg every other day did not fully block hydromorphone 24 mg intramuscularly (Greenwald et al., 2002).
key_findings.locator: 4.2.1, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: The intravenous-heroin finding is attributed to an earlier study by Comer et al. (2005), a description that fits neither that study as described on p. 4 nor the word earlier (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Summary: withdrawal suppression appears to require µOR availability of 50% or less, with trough plasma buprenorphine of at least 1 ng/mL; blockade of reinforcing and subjective effects has not been reliably observed under the doses studied; preliminary modelling suggests that blocking typical doses of other opioids would need availability below 20% (trough at least 3 ng/mL), and below 10% against higher-than-usual doses.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Results (p. 1); 4.3 Summary (p. 8)
key_findings.note: The abstract states the thresholds as results without the Summary's qualifiers; the body says neither threshold is known (2.2.1, PDF p. 3).

key_findings.finding: The authors state that there is no gold-standard definition of clinically meaningful blockade, and that the receptor availability needed for withdrawal suppression or for blockade, and how it varies with patients, opioids and routes, is not known.
key_findings.locator: 2.2.1 Definition of “opioid blockade”, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: PET measures began 4 h after the daily dose, the earliest time studied, and probably miss the largest reduction in availability; peak brain levels have to be inferred from plasma, because within-day PET time courses were not feasible.
key_findings.locator: 2.1.1, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Pharmacokinetics cited: plasma buprenorphine peaks about 1 h after a sublingual dose (Tmax 0.9–1.2 h) and norbuprenorphine at 1.4–1.6 h; mean half-life 21.7 h (SD 8.2) in the time-course study; in a study of 36 days of dosing, elimination half-life varied 3-fold for buprenorphine (24–69 h) and 8-fold for norbuprenorphine (22–176 h) (Kuhlman et al., 1998); after a first dose in healthy people, Tmax ranged 0.5–3.5 h and coefficients of variation for Cmax 31% to 84% (Elkader and Sproule, 2005).
key_findings.locator: 2.2.3 Buprenorphine-related factors, 2nd–3rd paragraphs (the 3rd continues on p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Variation between people: in the 2003 study, coefficients of variation at 16 and 32 mg/day were 24% and 21% for µOR availability, 39% and 54% for plasma levels and 129% and 109% for withdrawal symptoms; availability varied 3.5-fold in most regions at 2 mg/day, and individuals differed in how withdrawal related to availability.
key_findings.locator: 2.2.3, 8th paragraph (p. 4); 4.1, 3rd paragraph (p. 7)

key_findings.finding: In the time-course study, heavier smokers (20 or more cigarettes/day, n=5) had significantly lower µOR availability across regions and times than lighter smokers (15 or fewer/day, n=5), and reported more withdrawal, craving and response to hydromorphone after stopping; the authors say the small sample prevents firm conclusions.
key_findings.locator: 3. Results, 8th paragraph (starts p. 5, continues p. 7); Fig. 4 and legend (p. 7)

key_findings.finding: Medicines and conditions that raise buprenorphine levels could in theory cause toxicity (its partial agonist action may protect), and those that lower them could bring on withdrawal; the review lists drugs said to inhibit (atazanavir, ketoconazole, rifampin, possibly fluvoxamine) or induce (phenobarbital) its CYP3A4 metabolism.
key_findings.locator: 2.2.3, 5th–6th paragraphs
key_findings.note: Rifampin's place among the inhibitors is questioned in the reporting issues.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives µOR availability at 8 mg/day as 20–35%, while the legend of Fig. 1 and its dashed lines give 12–33% for the same estimate.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either figure may be quoted for 8 mg/day; their lower bounds differ by 8 points, and neither is a measurement (8 mg/day was not studied).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1, note b, says that values for doses not studied are in italics, but no value in Table 1 is italicized (checked on the page rendered at 300 dpi); only the text and the data points of Fig. 1 (left panel) show that 2, 16 and 32 mg/day were studied. The 1 mg/day estimate lies below the studied range (2–32 mg/day), and the text calls the range of estimates 16-fold although the table spans 1 to 32 mg/day.
reporting_issues.consequence: Curve-fit estimates (1, 4, 8, 12 and 24 mg/day) can be mistaken for measurements; the 1 mg/day value is an extrapolation.

reporting_issues.issue: The same time-course data appear as two different series: Table 1 (against the 2003 placebo condition: 27–31% at 4 h, 54–61% at 28 h) and the text (adjusted: 13–25% at 4 h, 37–46% at 24 h). The text says the 4-h values were adjusted to the identical condition of the 2003 study, yet the adjusted 4-h range (13–25%) does not match that study's 16 mg/day value in Table 1 (9–20%).
reporting_issues.consequence: A claim must say which series it cites; the adjustment cannot be reproduced from the paper, and the authors themselves advise caution about absolute levels (Table 1, note c).

reporting_issues.issue: The values at 8, 12, 16, 24, 48 and 72 h after the last dose are introduced as what “these data show”, but scans were made only at 4, 28, 52 and 76 h.
reporting_issues.consequence: They are interpolations from fitted curves in 10 people, not observations.

reporting_issues.issue: The plasma level of about 14 ng/mL said to go with near-zero availability comes from exponential fits in which the maximum plasma concentration was constrained to 15 ng/mL or less for each participant.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure is bounded by the fitting constraint; it is not an observed concentration.

reporting_issues.issue: An earlier study by Comer et al. (2005) is described as testing 16 mg/day against intravenous heroin 12.5 mg and 25 mg, but the Comer et al. (2005) study described on p. 4 used intranasal heroin with 2/0.5, 8/2 and 32/8 mg/day; the reference list also holds Comer et al. (2001), on intravenous heroin self-administration with sublingual tablets.
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a mis-citation (perhaps of the 2001 study); the finding should be traced to its primary paper before it is cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says self-administration of heroin 100 mg decreased modestly at the three maintenance doses, but Fig. 3 (upper right) shows control-group data only for 12.5 mg and 50 mg, so there is no reference without buprenorphine for 100 mg; in the figure, 100 mg self-administration stays high at all three levels (values not extracted).
reporting_issues.consequence: The decrease at 100 mg cannot be checked from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Rifampin is listed among drugs that inhibit buprenorphine metabolism by CYP3A4.
reporting_issues.consequence: Editors' note: rifampin is generally classed as an inducer of CYP3A4, which would lower buprenorphine levels rather than raise them; this list should not be cited for interactions without a pharmacology source.
