design_detail: Cross-sectional self-report survey of 1,679 people entering treatment for opioid use disorder at 49 US addiction treatment facilities, collected at routine admission by a third-party outcomes-tracking system (Trac9, NLW Partners, LLC) and analysed de-identified. The 1,163 who said they probably or definitely used fentanyl were asked the shortest time they had ever waited after fentanyl before taking buprenorphine (and, as a comparator, methadone), whether they had experienced withdrawal symptoms (none, mild, moderate, severe) when taking it after fentanyl, and whether it decreased their withdrawal. Severe withdrawal was compared across waiting-time categories by binary logistic regression; no covariates are reported and the reference category is not named (the editors reproduce every printed odds ratio exactly with the within-1-month group as reference). Survey dates, questionnaire wording and response rate are not reported. Read from the PMC author manuscript.
can_establish: How often people entering treatment who said they used fentanyl recalled severe withdrawal after taking buprenorphine (or methadone) after fentanyl, and how that recall varied with the shortest wait after fentanyl that they reported.
cannot_establish: The incidence of precipitated withdrawal (withdrawal brought on by buprenorphine is not separated from withdrawal it failed to relieve, and the occasion, dose, formulation and supervision are unknown), that waiting longer prevents it (the shortest wait ever is not tied to the occasion of the withdrawal and nothing is adjusted), or how often it occurs with supervised standard or low-dose starts.

sample.recruitment: Clinic: people entering treatment for opioid use disorder at one of 49 US addiction treatment facilities; a third-party aggregation system (Trac9, NLW Partners, LLC) collected the data to track treatment outcomes as part of routine admissions (Methods, Sample and Assessments, PDF p. 2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: The fentanyl questions were asked of people whose primary drug was opioids and who reported probably or definitely using fentanyl before treatment (PDF p. 2). No other criteria, survey period, facility types or states are reported.
sample.demographics: Of the 1,163 who reported fentanyl use: mean age 30.77 years (SD 10.23), 70.6% male (821), 80.4% White (935); 43.9% (510) said their urine tested positive for fentanyl at admission (Results, Patient Demographics, PDF p. 3). The paragraph opens with the 1,679, but these percentages are of the 1,163 (editors' calculation); the whole cohort is not described.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single survey). No response rate or item-completion figures are reported.
sample.selection_effects: People entering treatment at facilities using one outcomes system, which are not described; two authors are affiliated with Ashley Addiction Treatment. People who used fentanyl but did not enter these programmes are absent. Of the 1,163, 421 (36.2%) had never taken buprenorphine after fentanyl, and the 57 whose shortest wait was within a year are not in the withdrawal denominators (685 of the 742 who had ever taken it after fentanyl; editors' calculation) (Table 1, PDF p. 7). Recall at treatment entry may favour memorable bad experiences.

exposure.measurement: Self-report: fentanyl use (probably or definitely); the shortest time ever waited after fentanyl before taking buprenorphine or methadone, in categories within 24 h, 48 h, 72 h, 1 week, 1 month or 1 year, or never (Methods, PDF p. 2; Table 1, PDF p. 7). Urine fentanyl at admission only as reported by the respondent.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not recorded: the buprenorphine dose and formulation (the table note lists sublingual, buccal, transdermal, injectable and implant brands), whether it was prescribed and supervised or obtained otherwise, and how many times it was taken after fentanyl.
exposure.polysubstance: Not measured or reported (other opioids, sedatives, stimulants or adulterants).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; the time since fentanyl before buprenorphine is the exposure, recalled as the shortest wait ever.

comparison.controls: Within the survey: waiting-time categories compared with an unnamed reference category, which the editors' reproduction identifies as the people whose shortest wait was within 1 month (37 for buprenorphine, of whom 5 recalled severe withdrawal; 8 for methadone, of whom 2); methadone taken after fentanyl as a comparator medication; and the 152 who had taken both.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Amount, frequency and duration of fentanyl use, tolerance, whether withdrawal had already begun before buprenorphine was taken, buprenorphine dose and setting, and other drugs used.

outcomes.instruments: A single self-rated item on withdrawal symptoms when taking buprenorphine or methadone after fentanyl (none, mild, moderate, severe) and a single item on whether the medication decreased withdrawal (no, mild or moderate decrease, complete alleviation) (Table 1, PDF p. 7). No validated withdrawal scale; the question wording is not given in the paper (descriptive statistics are in Appendix 1, not among the files).
outcomes.validity_norms: None reported; retrospective recall of an unspecified occasion or occasions.
outcomes.operationalization: Precipitated withdrawal is taken to be self-rated severe withdrawal after taking buprenorphine following fentanyl. The survey does not separate withdrawal brought on by buprenorphine from withdrawal it failed to relieve; the authors themselves explain severe withdrawal after methadone as insufficient opioid effect (Discussion, 2nd paragraph, PDF p. 4).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: 8 odds ratios (4 waiting-time categories by 2 medications) at p<0.05.

analysis.effect_sizes: Withdrawal after buprenorphine taken after fentanyl (N=685, the people whose shortest wait was within 1 month): severe 250 (36.5%), moderate 136 (19.9%), mild 122 (17.8%), none 177 (25.8%); after methadone (N=200): severe 30 (15.0%), moderate 29 (14.5%), mild 44 (22.0%), none 97 (48.5%) (Table 1, PDF p. 7). Odds ratios for severe withdrawal with buprenorphine: within 24 h 5.202 (95% CI 1.979–13.675), p=0.001; within 48 h 3.352 (1.237–9.089), p=0.017; within 72 h 2.222 (0.780–6.329), p=0.135; within 1 week 2.133 (0.687–6.620), p=0.190; with methadone (N=199): 0.616 (0.117–3.247), 0.300 (0.035–2.606), 0.316 (0.036–2.750), 0.250 (0.019–3.342) (Table 1, PDF pp. 7–8). Editors' calculation: every printed odds ratio, interval and p value is reproduced exactly by unadjusted 2×2 comparisons against the within-1-month group, using the Table 1 group sizes, the printed severe counts for under 24 h (152) and 24–48 h (55), and severe counts of 25, 13 and 5 at 48–72 h, 72 h–1 week and 1 week–1 month (methadone 23, 2, 2, 1 and 2), which also match the bars of Figure 1 (measured at 300 dpi) and add up to 250 and 30. On these counts, the share recalling severe withdrawal within each waiting group was, for buprenorphine, 44.8% under 24 h (152/339; Wilson 95% CI 39.6–50.2), 34.4% at 24–48 h (55/160), 25.8% at 48–72 h (25/97), 25.0% at 72 h–1 week (13/52) and 13.5% at 1 week–1 month (5/37); for methadone 17.0% (23/135), 9.1% (2/22), 9.5% (2/21), 7.7% (1/13) and 25.0% (2/8). Overall proportions (Wilson 95% CI, editors): 36.5% (33.0–40.2) after buprenorphine and 15.0% (10.7–20.6) after methadone.
analysis.covariates: None reported (the reproduction shows the odds ratios are unadjusted).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: The questionnaire wording, survey period and descriptive statistics are in Appendix 1 (not among the files); the reference category of the regression is not named; the severe-withdrawal counts for the 72-h, 1-week and 1-month groups appear only as bars in Figure 1.
analysis.power: Not reported. The reference groups (37 and 8 people, by the editors' reproduction) make every odds ratio imprecise, the methadone ones extremely so.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Of 685 people entering treatment who said they had taken buprenorphine within a month after using fentanyl, 250 (36.5%) recalled severe withdrawal when they took it, against 30 of 200 (15.0%) after methadone. Recall of severe withdrawal was more common the shorter the shortest reported wait: about 45% when it was under 24 h, 34% at 24–48 h, about 25% at 48 h to 1 week and 14% at 1 week to 1 month (editors' calculation from the printed counts and odds ratios).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and results say that, of those who waited less than 24 hours, 22.19% reported severe withdrawal; that figure is 152 of all 685, not of the 339 who waited less than 24 hours, of whom 44.8% did (editors' calculation) (PDF pp. 1, 3). The objective speaks of incidence (PDF p. 1) and the conclusion of greater risk relative to those who wait more than 48 hours (PDF p. 4), but the data are recalled at treatment entry, the shortest wait ever is not tied to the occasion of the withdrawal, nothing is adjusted, and the comparison group is the 37 people whose shortest wait was 1 week to 1 month; people whose shortest wait was 48 h to 1 week still recalled severe withdrawal in about a quarter of cases (odds ratios about 2, not statistically significant), which the results call “no increase in odds” (PDF p. 3). Severe withdrawal after buprenorphine is labelled precipitated, although the survey cannot separate it from withdrawal that buprenorphine did not relieve, as the authors' own explanation of severe withdrawal after methadone shows (PDF p. 4). The discussion says buprenorphine preceded severe withdrawal in more than a third of the 1,163; the third is of 685 (PDF p. 3).

timeline.event: A qualitative study of buprenorphine experiences in the fentanyl era (Silverstein et al., 2019) and a commentary (Bisaga, 2019) are cited as the anecdotal evidence this survey supports (Discussion, 2nd paragraph, PDF p. 4).

A report of a method for starting people who use illicit fentanyl on buprenorphine/naloxone (Antoine et al., 2020, with Huhn) is cited among the case studies of precipitated withdrawal despite 2 to 3 days of observed abstinence (PDF p. 2).
The authors' study of protracted renal clearance of fentanyl in people with opioid use disorder (Huhn et al., 2020) is cited for the proposed mechanism (PDF p. 4).
Multisite emergency-department trial of buprenorphine starts reporting the incidence of precipitated withdrawal (title from the reference record; not read for this card)

replication.where_it_stands: The paper describes the earlier evidence as case reports and anecdotal accounts and cites no other survey. It cannot give the incidence of precipitated withdrawal at supervised starts; a later multisite trial in emergency departments is on the project's reference list (D'Onofrio et al., 2023) but was not read for this card.

funding.declared_conflicts: The authors report no conflicts of interest (PDF p. 1).

Crescenz VA Medical Center); Hobelmann and Huhn are also affiliated with Ashley Addiction Treatment, a treatment provider, and the data came from NLW Partners' Trac9 system, both named in the disclaimer. Two cited background studies are the authors' own (references 2 and 7), as is one of the low-dose induction papers (reference 13). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study of buprenorphine starts in people who use fentanyl that records the time since last fentanyl use (with urine fentanyl and norfentanyl), withdrawal on a validated scale before and after the first doses, the dose, formulation and setting, and compares standard with low-dose starts, ideally by randomization.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Admissions to 49 US treatment facilities using one outcomes-tracking system suit the stated population of people entering treatment, but the facilities, states and period are not described, and people who use fentanyl outside these programmes are not in the frame.
Data came from routine admissions; whether every admission was asked, and how many answered, is not reported.

685 and 200 give the overall proportions reasonable precision (36.5%, Wilson 95% CI 33.0–40.2; 15.0%, 10.7–20.6; editors' calculation), but the odds ratios rest on reference groups of 37 and 8 people (editors' reproduction).

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Only the age, sex, race and self-reported urine fentanyl of the 1,163 are given; facility type, setting, states, survey dates and questionnaire wording are not.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: No response or item-completion figures; the 57 whose shortest wait was within a year are outside the withdrawal denominators without explanation; the methadone denominator is 200 in one part of Table 1 and 199 in another.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Precipitated withdrawal is identified by one self-rated item recalled for an unspecified occasion; no validated scale; withdrawal brought on by buprenorphine is not distinguished from withdrawal it did not relieve.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: The same questionnaire at admission for everyone, but reliability is not reported and answers refer to different occasions, doses and settings.

Key percentages are given with the wrong denominators in the abstract and results; the logistic regression is unadjusted with an unnamed reference group; no intervals for the proportions; the conclusion compares with people who waited more than 48 hours, who were not the reference group.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: Response rate not reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI has no overall algorithm; the editors' summary is high risk of bias. The survey reports on a large group of people entering treatment, but its outcome is a single recalled rating that cannot separate precipitated from unrelieved withdrawal, its sample frame and response are not described, its timing comparison is unadjusted and tied to the shortest wait ever rather than to the occasion, and its headline percentages use the wrong denominators. It may be cited for this: among people entering treatment who said they used fentanyl and had taken buprenorphine within a month after fentanyl, about a third (36.5%) recalled severe withdrawal, against 15% after methadone, and recall of severe withdrawal was more common the shorter the shortest wait (from about 45% under 24 h to about 14% at 1 week to 1 month; editors' calculation). It should not be cited for the incidence of precipitated withdrawal at supervised starts, for a safe waiting time, or for 22% as the rate among those who waited less than 24 hours.

key_findings.finding: Survey of 1,679 people entering treatment for opioid use disorder at 49 US addiction treatment facilities, collected by a third-party outcomes-tracking system (Trac9) at routine admission and analysed de-identified; the fentanyl questions went to those whose primary drug was opioids and who reported probably or definitely using fentanyl.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Methods (p. 1); Methods, Sample and Assessments (p. 2)

key_findings.finding: 1,163 (69.3%) reported probably (180; 10.7%) or definitely (983; 58.5%) using fentanyl before treatment; they had a mean age of 30.77 years (SD 10.23), were 70.6% male (821) and 80.4% White (935), and 43.9% (510) said their urine tested positive for fentanyl at admission.
key_findings.locator: Results, Patient Demographics

key_findings.finding: Shortest wait after fentanyl before taking buprenorphine (N=1,163): within 24 h 339 (29.1%), within 48 h 160 (13.8%), within 72 h 97 (8.3%), within 1 week 52 (4.5%), within 1 month 37 (3.2%), within 1 year 57 (4.9%), never 421 (36.2%). For methadone: 135 (11.6%), 22 (1.9%), 21 (1.8%), 13 (1.1%), 8 (0.7%), 29 (2.5%), never 935 (80.4%).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, first panel

key_findings.finding: Of the 685 who had taken buprenorphine within a month after fentanyl, 250 (36.5%) recalled severe withdrawal, 136 (19.9%) moderate, 122 (17.8%) mild and 177 (25.8%) none; of 200 who had taken methadone, 30 (15.0%) severe, 29 (14.5%) moderate, 44 (22.0%) mild and 97 (48.5%) none.
key_findings.locator: Results, Survey Results (p. 3); Table 1, second panel (p. 7)
key_findings.note: 685 equals the buprenorphine groups up to 1 month (339+160+97+52+37), so the 57 whose shortest wait was within a year are not included (editors' calculation). Wilson 95% CI 33.0–40.2% for buprenorphine and 10.7–20.6% for methadone (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: As printed, 22.19% (152 of 685) of the buprenorphine group and 11.56% (23 of 199) of the methadone group had waited less than 24 hours and recalled severe withdrawal; 8.03% (55 of 685) and 1.01% (2 of 199) had waited 24–48 hours and recalled severe withdrawal.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Results (p. 1); Results, Odds of Severe Opioid Withdrawal, 2nd paragraph (p. 3)
key_findings.note: The paper words these as rates among those who waited less than 24 (or 48) hours; they are shares of all 685 (or 199). Within each group (editors' calculation from the Table 1 group sizes): 152 of 339 (44.8%) and 55 of 160 (34.4%) for buprenorphine; 23 of 135 (17.0%) and 2 of 22 (9.1%) for methadone.

key_findings.locator: Results, Odds of Severe Opioid Withdrawal, 1st paragraph (p. 3); Table 1, fourth panel (pp. 7–8)
key_findings.note: The reference category is not named. Editors' calculation: all eight odds ratios, intervals and p values are reproduced exactly by unadjusted comparisons with the within-1-month group (37 people, 5 with severe withdrawal, for buprenorphine; 8 people, 2, for methadone).

key_findings.finding: Editors' calculation from Table 1, the printed odds ratios and Figure 1: severe withdrawal was recalled by 25 of 97 (25.8%) whose shortest wait was 48–72 h, 13 of 52 (25.0%) at 72 h to 1 week and 5 of 37 (13.5%) at 1 week to 1 month for buprenorphine, and by 2 of 21, 1 of 13 and 2 of 8 for methadone; with the printed counts for shorter waits these add up to the totals of 250 and 30.
key_findings.locator: Figure 1, left panel (p. 6); Table 1 (pp. 7–8)
key_findings.note: Not printed as numbers: reconstructed from the odds ratios and confirmed by the Figure 1 bars measured at 300 dpi (buprenorphine 3.63%, 1.87% and 0.72% of 685; methadone 1.0%, 0.49% and 1.0% of 199).

key_findings.finding: Among the 152 who had taken both medications after fentanyl, 69 (45.4%) recalled severe withdrawal after buprenorphine and 20 (13.2%) after methadone.
key_findings.locator: Results, Odds of Severe Opioid Withdrawal, 2nd paragraph (p. 3); Figure 1, right panel (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: Complete relief of withdrawal was reported by 68 of 177 (38.4%) for buprenorphine and 43 of 97 (44.3%) for methadone; no decrease by 29 (16.4%) and 18 (18.6%).
key_findings.locator: Results, Survey Results (p. 3); Table 1, third panel (p. 7)
key_findings.note: The denominators (177 and 97) equal the numbers who reported no withdrawal symptoms after each medication; the paper does not say who was asked this question.

key_findings.finding: 483 of the 1,163 (41.5%) knew someone who used fentanyl and had precipitated withdrawal after taking buprenorphine.
key_findings.locator: Results, Survey Results

key_findings.finding: In the introduction, the authors state that buprenorphine taken within 6 to 8 hours of a full agonist such as fentanyl can precipitate withdrawal by displacing it, and that case studies had reported precipitated withdrawal in people using fentanyl despite 2 to 3 days of observed abstinence.
key_findings.locator: Introduction (unheaded), 1st paragraph (p. 2); References 2–4 (p. 5)
key_findings.note: No source is cited for the 6–8 h statement; the case studies cited (references 2–4) include a 2003 article and a 2021 systematic review of micro-induction, by their titles (PDF p. 5).

key_findings.finding: The authors suggest that fentanyl accumulates in fat with repeated use and can take weeks to clear through the kidneys (citing their own study), and that buprenorphine displacing it may contribute to precipitated withdrawal within 48 hours of fentanyl use even when clinicians follow conventional induction procedures; they hypothesize that severe withdrawal after methadone may reflect poorly managed withdrawal from too little opioid effect early in treatment, since first outpatient doses are capped and methadone takes more than a week to reach steady levels.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Conclusion: people who take buprenorphine within 24 to 48 hours of fentanyl use are at significantly greater risk of severe withdrawal than those who wait more than 48 hours.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions
key_findings.note: Editors' reproduction: the model's reference group was the 37 people whose shortest wait was 1 week to 1 month, not everyone who waited more than 48 hours (see reporting issues).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and results give 22.19% (152/685) as the share reporting severe withdrawal among those who waited less than 24 hours, and 8.03% (55/685) among those who waited less than 48 hours; both use all 685 as the denominator. The same applies to methadone (11.56% = 23/199; 1.01% = 2/199).
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract halves the rate for the group it names. Editors' calculation: within the groups named, the shares are 44.8% (152/339) and 34.4% (55/160) for buprenorphine and 17.0% (23/135) and 9.1% (2/22) for methadone.

reporting_issues.issue: The Survey Results paragraph prints 29.1% (n=339/685) and 11.6% (n=135/200), but 29.1% and 11.6% are shares of 1,163, and its 36.5% (250/685) reads as if it referred to the 339 who waited less than 24 hours, whereas it refers to all 685.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paragraph is easily misread; Table 1 gives the right denominators. Editors' calculation: 339/685 would be 49.5% and 135/200 67.5%.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion says buprenorphine preceded severe withdrawal in more than a third of the 1,163 people who reported fentanyl use; the third is of the 685 who took buprenorphine within a month after fentanyl.
reporting_issues.consequence: Editors' calculation: of all 1,163, the 250 are 21.5%.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 1 (left) plots each waiting group's severe cases as a share of all 685 (or 199), so its fall from about 22% to under 1% mostly reflects the smaller numbers of people with longer waits (339 down to 37, Table 1), not lower risk; the legend does not explain this.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure should not be read as risk by waiting time. Editors' calculation: within-group shares fall from 44.8% to 13.5%.

reporting_issues.issue: The reference category of the logistic regression is not named, and the conclusion compares with people who wait more than 48 hours; the editors' exact reproduction of the odds ratios shows the reference was the 37 people whose shortest wait was within 1 month. People whose shortest wait was 48–72 h or 72 h to 1 week recalled severe withdrawal in about a quarter of cases (odds ratios 2.222 and 2.133, not significant), which the results describe as no increase in odds.
reporting_issues.consequence: The data show a gradient with time since fentanyl, not a safe point at 48 hours; the non-significant odds ratios reflect a reference group of 37.

reporting_issues.issue: The methadone denominator is 200 in the withdrawal-severity panel of Table 1 but 199 in the waiting-time panel and the odds model.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor. Editors' calculation: 30 severe cases are 15.0% of 200 or 15.1% of 199.

reporting_issues.issue: The denominators of the relief question (177 for buprenorphine, 97 for methadone) equal the numbers who reported no withdrawal symptoms after each medication; the paper does not say who was asked.
reporting_issues.consequence: If only people without withdrawal were asked, the comparison of complete relief (38.4% against 44.3%) concerns that subgroup only.

reporting_issues.issue: The objective is to estimate the incidence of buprenorphine-precipitated withdrawal, but the outcome is a single self-rated severity item recalled at treatment entry, not tied to the occasion of the shortest wait, without a validated scale.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figures are recalled lifetime proportions, not incidence, and they include withdrawal that buprenorphine did not relieve as well as withdrawal it brought on.

design_detail: Retrospective cohort study in the MarketScan multistate Medicaid claims database, 2013–2017 (about 12 million enrollees a year). Adults aged 18–64 who began a new buprenorphine episode (no buprenorphine claim in the previous 60 days), stayed on it continuously for at least 180 days, then stopped (a gap of more than 60 days beyond the days supplied; the last day of medication coverage counts as the day of stopping) and stayed enrolled for 6 months afterwards. The 8,996 people were grouped by how long they had stayed on buprenorphine (6–9, 9–12, 12–15 and 15–18 months). Outcomes in the 6 months after stopping: any emergency department visit, any inpatient admission, any filled full-agonist opioid prescription, and any medically treated drug overdose (opioid or non-opioid). Logistic regressions compared each longer group with the 6–9-month group, adjusted for age, sex, race/ethnicity, Medicaid plan type, psychiatric, alcohol and non-opioid drug use diagnoses, and initial buprenorphine dose. There is no group that stayed on buprenorphine. Appraised with ROBINS-I as a non-randomized comparison of treatment durations, as the round brief directs. Read from the online-first version (AJP in Advance).
can_establish: How often Medicaid enrollees who stopped buprenorphine after 6 to 18 months of continuous treatment had emergency visits, hospital admissions, full-agonist opioid prescriptions and medically treated overdoses in the next 6 months, and whether those who had stayed longer differed on these outcomes after adjustment for recorded characteristics.
cannot_establish: Whether stopping buprenorphine raises the risk of overdose compared with staying on it (no group that continued), whether longer treatment causes the better outcomes (people stopped at different times for reasons not recorded), how many overdoses were fatal (deaths are not recorded and people who died lost enrolment and were excluded), or whether the figures apply to people who stop in the first weeks or months, or outside Medicaid.

sample.recruitment: Registry: insurance claims and enrolment records of the MarketScan multistate Medicaid database, 2013–2017, including inpatient, outpatient, emergency and pharmacy claims billed to Medicaid (Methods, Study Design and Participants, 1st paragraph, PDF p. 2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Age 18–64 at initiation; a new episode after a 60-day baseline without buprenorphine claims; formulations approved for pain excluded; continuous buprenorphine for 180 to 545 days by days supplied; discontinuation within the study window, defined as a gap of more than 60 days beyond the days supplied; continuous Medicaid enrolment for 6 months after stopping; initiation before 1 January 2017 (Methods, PDF pp. 2–3; Figure 1 note, PDF p. 2). Flow: 26,576 with a continuous episode of more than 6 months; 10,481 who did not stop and 3,159 who stopped with less than 6 months left in the study window removed (12,936); 3,940 without continuous enrolment through the follow-up removed (8,996) (Results, 1st paragraph, PDF pp. 3–4; Figure 2, PDF p. 3).
sample.demographics: 61.0% women; 76.4% aged 25–44; 91.5% White; mean initial dose 8.0 mg/day (group means 7.9–8.2) (Results, 1st–2nd paragraphs, PDF pp. 3–4; Table 1, PDF p. 4). From the Table 1 totals (editors' calculation): psychiatric diagnosis 30.9%, alcohol use disorder 4.8%, non-opioid drug use disorder 21.7%.
sample.attrition: 3,940 of the 12,936 who stopped within the window (30.5%, editors' calculation) were excluded because they were not continuously enrolled in the 6 months after stopping; excluded and included people are not compared (Results, 1st paragraph, PDF pp. 3–4; Figure 2).
sample.selection_effects: Only people who reached 6 months of continuous treatment, whom the authors describe as a minority of Medicaid patients who start buprenorphine and as likely relatively stable (Discussion, 7th paragraph, PDF p. 6), and only those who stopped: 10,481 of 26,576 with such an episode (39.4%, editors' calculation) had not stopped and were excluded. The 6-month enrolment requirement after stopping removes people who died or lost Medicaid in that period; the authors state that people with fatal overdoses would have lost eligibility and been ineligible (PDF pp. 6–7). People also covered by Medicare were excluded (PDF p. 7).

exposure.measurement: Pharmacy claims: days supplied of buprenorphine formulations approved for opioid use disorder, from the index claim to the last fill before a gap of more than 60 days (Methods, Study Design and Participants, 3rd paragraph, PDF p. 3).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Duration groups by days supplied: 180–270, 271–364, 365–455 and 456–545 days (PDF p. 3). Initial dose recorded only as a group mean (7.9–8.2 mg/day; Table 1); formulation, later doses and whether medication was taken are not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Recorded only as diagnoses on the day of initiation or in the 60-day baseline: alcohol use disorder (ICD-10 F10) and non-opioid drug use disorders (F12–F16, F18–F19), both adjusted for; actual drug use not measured (Methods, Measures, 2nd paragraph, PDF p. 3).

comparison.controls: The 6–9-month group (n=4,126) is the reference for the 9–12, 12–15 and 15–18-month groups; no group continued buprenorphine (Figure 1 note, PDF p. 2; Methods, Statistical Analysis, PDF p. 3).
comparison.matching: None; regression adjustment for age group, sex, race/ethnicity (White or nonwhite), Medicaid plan type, psychiatric diagnosis, alcohol use disorder, non-opioid drug use disorder and initial buprenorphine dose (PDF p. 3).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Addiction severity, which the authors could not measure from claims (Discussion, 7th paragraph, PDF p. 6), reasons for stopping (planned taper, dropping out, cost or coverage limits, incarceration, moving), opioid use, housing and employment, and treatment after stopping (restarting buprenorphine, methadone, naltrexone).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The same diagnostic covariates for all groups.

outcomes.instruments: Claims in the 6 months after the last day of medication coverage: at least one all-cause emergency department visit; at least one all-cause inpatient admission; at least one filled full-agonist opioid prescription; at least one medically treated drug overdose, opioid or non-opioid, by ICD-10 codes printed as T36–T39 and T40.5–T50, with the full list in Table S1 of the online supplement, which was not among the files (Methods, Measures, 1st paragraph, PDF p. 3).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not reported. Claims capture only overdoses that reached billed care; deaths outside hospital are not captured.
outcomes.operationalization: Each outcome is binary (any event in 6 months). Full-agonist opioid prescriptions are read as a marker of relapse or poorly coordinated care (PDF p. 3), although they may also be prescribed for pain.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: 4 outcomes by 3 duration comparisons (12 adjusted odds ratios) at p<0.05, plus a sensitivity analysis.

analysis.effect_sizes: Unadjusted 6-month rates across the four groups: emergency visits 41.2–48.6%, inpatient admissions 11.3–13.9%, full-agonist opioid prescriptions 19.1–25.9%, medically treated overdoses 5.1–5.5%; overall, 464 of 8,996 (5.2%) had at least one overdose (Results, 3rd–4th paragraphs, PDF p. 4). 15–18 against 6–9 months, unadjusted: emergency visits 41.2% vs 48.6% (p<0.001), admissions 11.3% vs 13.9% (p<0.05), opioid prescriptions 19.1% vs 25.9% (p<0.001) (Results, 4th paragraph, PDF p. 4). Adjusted odds ratios (Table 2, PDF p. 6): 15–18 months, admissions 0.79 (95% CI 0.64–0.99), emergency visits 0.75 (0.65–0.86), overdose 1.04 (0.75–1.44), opioid prescriptions 0.67 (0.56–0.80); 12–15 months, 0.86 (0.72–1.03), 0.84 (0.75–0.95), 1.10 (0.84–1.43), 0.84 (0.73–0.97); 9–12 months, 0.86 (0.74–1.01), 0.94 (0.85–1.04), 1.04 (0.82–1.30), 0.95 (0.85–1.07). Sensitivity analysis with a documented opioid use disorder diagnosis (N=8,077), 15–18 against 6–9 months: emergency visits 0.74 (0.64–0.86), admissions 0.79 (0.63–0.99), opioid prescriptions 0.68 (0.56–0.82); overdose odds equivalent across groups, overall rate 5.6% (Results, 6th paragraph, PDF p. 5). Editors' calculation from the printed unadjusted rates, 15–18 against 6–9 months: 7.4 percentage points fewer with an emergency visit, 2.6 fewer admitted, 6.8 fewer with an opioid prescription; overdose 464/8,996 = 5.2% (Wilson 95% CI 4.7–5.6%).
analysis.covariates: Age group, sex, race/ethnicity, Medicaid plan type (fee for service or capitation), psychiatric diagnosis (ICD-10 F01–F09, F20–F99), alcohol use disorder, non-opioid drug use disorder, and initial buprenorphine dose as a continuous variable (Methods, PDF p. 3; Table 2, PDF p. 6).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol is mentioned. The authors state that the 3-month groupings were chosen before the analyses and that their hypothesis was set before the data were analysed (PDF pp. 2–3).
analysis.selective_reporting: All four primary outcomes are reported for all three comparisons (Table 2), and the null overdose result is in the abstract. The abstract's range for emergency visits (42.1–49.9%) differs from the Results (41.2–48.6%). Rates for the 9–12 and 12–15-month groups are shown only as bars in Figure 3; Tables S1–S3 are in the online supplement.
analysis.power: Not reported; the authors suggest that the null overdose result may reflect insufficient power (Discussion, 4th paragraph, PDF p. 5). The interval for the 15–18-month group (0.75–1.44) is compatible with odds of overdose 25% lower to 44% higher.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 8,996 Medicaid enrollees who stopped buprenorphine after 6 to 18 months and remained enrolled for 6 more months, 41–49% had an emergency visit, 11–14% a hospital admission, 19–26% a full-agonist opioid prescription and 5.2% at least one medically treated overdose in those 6 months. People who had stayed 15–18 months had lower adjusted odds of emergency visits, admissions and opioid prescriptions than those who stopped after 6–9 months, and the same odds of overdose.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the risk of acute care and overdose was high after stopping, whatever the duration, and that superior outcomes became significant beyond 15 months of treatment (abstract, PDF p. 1); but the study has no group that continued treatment, and the 12–15-month group already had significantly lower odds of emergency visits and opioid prescriptions (Table 2, PDF p. 6). The discussion says the study demonstrates that the period after stopping goes with overdose rates about two to three times those of a general sample of people with opioid use disorder (Discussion, 4th paragraph, PDF p. 5), citing a meta-analysis of death rates per 1000 person-years (reference 29, Sordo et al., 2017) without giving the figures compared or how a 6-month proportion of medically treated overdoses was made comparable. The authors' statement that fatal overdoses are unlikely to differ between groups (PDF p. 6) cannot be checked, since people who died were excluded by design. The conclusions concede that the design cannot establish a causal relationship (PDF p. 7), yet recommend longer treatment and changes to insurance and care systems.

timeline.event: Pennsylvania Medicaid cohort (Gordon et al., 2015, as cited): 21% persistently refilled buprenorphine for 12 months; against people who persisted only 3–5 months, they had an 18% lower risk of hospitalization and a 14% lower risk of emergency department use (Discussion, 6th paragraph, PDF p. 6).
Meta-analysis of mortality during and after opioid substitution treatment, cited for the claim that overdose rates after stopping are two to three times those of a general sample

Cohort after non-fatal overdose (Larochelle et al., 2018, as cited): an approximate annual rate of 5% to 7.5% for subsequent overdoses, with which the authors compare their 6-month rate (Discussion, 5th paragraph, PDF p. 5).

replication.where_it_stands: No direct replication is described in the paper or known from the files read for this card. The finding that about 5 in 100 had a medically treated overdose within 6 months of stopping comes from one claims database and excludes deaths; whether stopping raises overdose risk compared with continuing needs studies that link deaths and include people who continue.

The paper argues for longer treatment and for insurance and care-system changes, and cites the authors' earlier work on a treatment cascade, quality measures and discontinuation (references 3, 5, 16 and 31). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A cohort that links treatment or claims records to death records, so that fatal overdoses are counted and people are not lost when their insurance ends, comparing people who stop buprenorphine with similar people who continue over the same calendar time, with reasons for stopping and later treatment recorded; or a randomized trial of continued treatment against a planned taper after a set duration, with overdose and death as outcomes.

domains.note: Duration was not assigned: people who stop after 6–9 months may differ in severity, stability, circumstances and reasons for stopping. Adjustment covers only demographics, plan type, initial dose and diagnoses recorded at baseline; no measure of severity (the authors say none was available, PDF p. 6) and no time-varying factors.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Entry required stopping within the window and then 6 months of continuous enrolment after stopping, a condition observed after the start of follow-up: anyone who died, including from overdose, or lost Medicaid in those 6 months was excluded.

Duration and the date of stopping are derived from fill dates and days supplied with a 60-day gap rule; fills do not show whether medication was taken, and restarting after the gap within the outcome window is not described.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Treatment after stopping (restarting buprenorphine, methadone or naltrexone) is not reported and may differ between groups.

3,940 of 12,936 (30.5%) were excluded for incomplete enrolment in the outcome period; loss of enrolment can follow death, a direct consequence of the outcome; excluded and included people are not compared.

Claims-based outcomes do not depend on knowledge of the group, but capture only billed events; fatal overdoses outside hospital are missed; the printed overdose codes omit T40.0–T40.4 (see reporting issues); opioid prescriptions may reflect pain care.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: All four outcomes are reported for all comparisons, including the null result for overdose, and the groupings were set before analysis (PDF p. 3).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The 6-month rates are reliable descriptions of the people included (Medicaid enrollees who stopped after at least 6 months and stayed enrolled for 6 more), but they are not the full risk after stopping, because deaths and loss of Medicaid removed people from the analysis. The comparison between durations is open to confounding by why and when people stopped. The study may be cited for how common emergency care, full-agonist opioid prescriptions and medically treated overdoses were in the 6 months after stopping long-term buprenorphine in this population, and for the absence of a detectable difference in overdose by duration; it cannot be cited for overdose risk after stopping compared with continuing, for fatal overdose, or for longer treatment causing better outcomes.

key_findings.finding: Cohort: 8,996 Medicaid enrollees aged 18–64 (MarketScan multistate claims, 2013–2017) who stopped buprenorphine after at least 180 days of continuous treatment and stayed enrolled for 6 months afterwards: 4,126 had been treated 6–9 months, 2,440 for 9–12 months, 1,499 for 12–15 months and 931 for 15–18 months.
key_findings.locator: Methods, Study Design and Participants, 1st–3rd paragraphs (pp. 2–3); Figure 2 (p. 3); Results, 2nd paragraph and Table 1 (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Of 26,576 people with a new continuous buprenorphine episode of more than 6 months, 10,481 did not stop and 3,159 stopped with less than 6 months left in the study window; of the remaining 12,936, 3,940 were excluded because they were not continuously enrolled through the 6 months after stopping.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (starts p. 3, continues p. 4); Figure 2 (p. 3)

key_findings.finding: The people included were 61.0% women, 76.4% aged 25–44 and 91.5% White; the mean initial buprenorphine dose was 8.0 mg/day (group means 7.9–8.2 mg/day); nonwhite people were slightly less likely to be in the 15–18-month group (p=0.04).
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st–2nd paragraphs; Table 1 (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: In the 6 months after stopping, across the four duration groups, 41.2–48.6% had an emergency department visit, 11.3–13.9% an inpatient admission, 19.1–25.9% filled a full-agonist opioid prescription, and 5.1–5.5% had at least one medically treated overdose.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Figure 3 (p. 5)
key_findings.note: The abstract (PDF p. 1) gives 42.1–49.9% for emergency visits (see reporting issues). Overdoses counted are those of people still enrolled 6 months after stopping.

key_findings.finding: Overall, 464 of 8,996 people (5.2%) had at least one medically treated overdose (opioid or non-opioid) in the 6 months after stopping buprenorphine; overdose was not related to how long they had been treated (6 to 18 months).
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Unadjusted, the 15–18-month group had fewer emergency visits (41.2% vs 48.6%, p<0.001), admissions (11.3% vs 13.9%, p<0.05) and opioid prescription claims (19.1% vs 25.9%, p<0.001) than the 6–9-month group; overdose was comparable across all groups.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph (p. 4); Figure 3 (p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Adjusted odds ratios against the 6–9-month group: 15–18 months, emergency visits 0.75 (95% CI 0.65–0.86), admissions 0.79 (0.64–0.99), opioid prescriptions 0.67 (0.56–0.80), overdose 1.04 (0.75–1.44); 12–15 months, emergency visits 0.84 (0.75–0.95) and opioid prescriptions 0.84 (0.73–0.97), admissions 0.86 (0.72–1.03), overdose 1.10 (0.84–1.43); 9–12 months, no significant difference (overdose 1.04, 0.82–1.30).
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph (starts p. 4, continues p. 5); Table 2 (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: In the same models, overdose after stopping was less likely in women (OR 0.65, 95% CI 0.54–0.79) and more likely with a psychiatric diagnosis (1.61, 1.32–1.96), alcohol use disorder (2.02, 1.47–2.79) or a non-opioid drug use disorder (1.51, 1.22–1.86); initial dose was not related (1.00 per mg, 0.97–1.04).
key_findings.locator: Table 2, Overdose columns

key_findings.finding: Restricted to the 8,077 people with a documented opioid use disorder diagnosis, the 15–18-month group again had lower odds of emergency visits (0.74, 0.64–0.86), admissions (0.79, 0.63–0.99) and opioid prescriptions (0.68, 0.56–0.82); overdose odds were equivalent across groups, with 5.6% overall having an overdose in the 6 months after stopping.
key_findings.locator: Results, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: no data on vital status, so fatal and non-fatal overdoses could not be told apart; people who died of overdose during treatment or in the 6 months after stopping would have lost Medicaid eligibility and were therefore not in the analysis; residual confounding is possible and addiction severity could not be measured; results are limited to Medicaid enrollees without Medicare, and the states contributing data are not named.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 7th paragraph (starts p. 6, continues p. 7)

key_findings.finding: Stopping was defined as a gap of more than 60 days beyond the days supplied by the last fill, dated to the last day of medication coverage, so the 6-month outcome window includes the first 60 days without a buprenorphine fill.
key_findings.locator: Figure 1 note (p. 2); Methods, Study Design and Participants, 3rd paragraph (p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Medically treated overdose was defined by ICD-10 codes printed as T36–T39 and T40.5–T50 (opioid and non-opioid), with the full list in Table S1 of the online supplement; a full-agonist opioid prescription is described as generally contraindicated with buprenorphine and as a marker of relapse or poorly coordinated care.
key_findings.locator: Methods, Measures, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: See reporting issues on the printed code range; Table S1 was not among the files.

key_findings.finding: The discussion states that overdose rates after stopping were about two to three times those observed in a general sample of people with opioid use disorder (reference 29), giving no figures for that comparison, and that the overdose rate in the sample lay within an approximate annual rate of 5% to 7.5% for subsequent overdoses reported for people with a past-year overdose (reference 2).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th and 5th paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives 42.1–49.9% for emergency department visits; the Results give 41.2–48.6%, matching the bars of Figure 3.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the Results range.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and conclusions place the benefit of longer treatment beyond 15 months (a minimum of 15–18 months), but the 12–15-month group already had significantly lower adjusted odds of emergency visits (0.84, 0.75–0.95) and opioid prescriptions (0.84, 0.73–0.97).
reporting_issues.consequence: The threshold of 15 months is a simplification; the data show a gradient for two outcomes.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion says opioid prescription claims averaged more than 25% across groups, but the Results range is 19.1–25.9%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Editors' reading of Figure 3 (bars calibrated on the gridlines; about 25.9%, 25.2%, 23.0% and 19.2%) gives a weighted average of about 24.5%; the statement slightly overstates the rate.

reporting_issues.issue: The overdose code list is printed as T36–T39, T40.5–T50 although the same sentence says opioid overdoses were counted.
reporting_issues.consequence: Editors' note: in ICD-10, T40.0–T40.4 are the codes for poisoning by opium, heroin, other opioids, methadone and other synthetic narcotics, so the printed range would leave out opioid overdoses. Probably a typesetting error; Table S1 of the online supplement (not among the files) gives the codes used and should be read before the overdose figure is cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The limitations say that fatal and non-fatal overdoses could not be told apart, and also that people who died of overdose would have lost eligibility and been excluded; the authors then reason that fatal overdoses are unlikely to differ between groups because overdoses occurred at similar rates.
reporting_issues.consequence: The overdoses counted are mostly those of people who survived and stayed enrolled; fatal overdoses after stopping are largely outside the data, and their distribution by group cannot be inferred from non-fatal ones.

reporting_issues.issue: The claim that overdose rates after stopping are about two to three times those of a general sample of people with opioid use disorder gives no figures; its source (reference 29, Sordo et al., 2017) pooled death rates per 1000 person-years (card sc_sordo_2017), whereas this study counts medically treated overdoses, fatal or not, as a 6-month proportion.
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparison cannot be checked and compares different outcomes; it should not be cited as a finding of this study.

reporting_issues.issue: The 6-month overdose proportion (5.2%) is compared with annual rates of 5% to 7.5% after a past-year overdose.
reporting_issues.consequence: A 6-month proportion compared with annual rates understates the comparison; no adjustment for the length of follow-up is made.
